As I understand that this motion
is for the house to go into committee of supply for the purpose of considering the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I desire to bring to the attention of the house the case of the dismissal of one Mr. Couture, of St. Bernard, Dorchester county, from his office as inspector of weights and measures, which is under a sub-department or branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I desire at the same time to present facts in connection with this dismissal, which I trust will justify the Minister of Trade and Commerce in granting an inquiry into the charges which have been alleged against this official and which were the grounds for his dismissal. I also intend before closing my address to move an amendment to this motion to go into supply, dealing generally with the matter of dismissals for partisan political activities.
I may state at the outset that in proposing this amendment I a;m not proposing a vote of want of confidence in the government; I trust that the amendment will so commend itself to the government that they will be prepared to accept it. Paragraph 489 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms makes it clearly apparent that the acceptance of this amendment will not prevent the house from going into committee of supply at the present time. That paragraph reads:
When an amendment has been adopted to the motion for the house to go into committee of supply or of ways and means, it may be forthwith moved that the house resolve itself into sueh committee immediately or on a future day.
So that the acceptance of the amendment which I propose would not prevent the house from going into committee of supply on ihe estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
During the last session I had occasion to bring to the attention of the house the case of an official of the Department of National Revenue, one Dumoulin, of Notre Dame des Bois, in the province of Quebec. I wish now to pay tribute to the minister of that department (Mr. Euler), for the manner in which he fulfilled the promise which he made on that occasion. He declared that under the circumstances disclosed in that discussion he believed that Dumoulin should have an opportunity of appearing before a com-
missioner to prove his innocence of the charges made against him by a member of this parliament. He also stated that, if the innocence of the dismissed employee was proved, he would see, in so far as it lay within his power, that there should be redress- not that the official should be reinstated in office, because the minister held that there was a ruling of the Department of Justice that a minister, after the dismissal of an official, had no power to reappoint him to the same office. But th,e Minister of National Revenue did declare on that occasion that if on inquiry this official proved his innocence he would have the man reinstated in some other similar office. The minister ordered an inquiry, which was duly held. Evidence was taken and it proved the entire innocence of the dismissed official. I wish to say in commendation of the minister that he did thereupon recommend for appointment the exofficial Dumoulin who had been so dismissed. It is true that Dumoulin on that occasion was compelled again to stand examination before the Civil Service Commission; It is true Be was appointed, not to the same but to a similar office; it is probable that although he was proved to be innocent he lost his interest in the superannuation fund to which he had contributed for so many years before his dismissal; and unless the law is changed I do not think there is any doubt that he will lose the priority which he had attained by reason of several years of service in that department-all of which are grave disadvantages accruing from a dismissal which now admittedly had been improperly made.
I have therefore looked into the law with respect to the dismissal of officials, not only in Great Britain but in this country. I find that in Great Britain, as in Canada, the executive and administrative powers of the Privy Council include all those matters which, under our constitution, are entrusted to the sovereign by virtue of the royal prerogative. His Excellency the Governor General acts, in the exercise of that royal prerogative in respect of the domestic affairs of this country, on the advice of the Privy Council of Canada. In Canada those orders in council which are expressed to be made on the recommendation of a committee of the Privy Council and to be approved by the Governor General, make appointments to office, remove from office officials appointed during the pleasure of the crown, and accept resignations and order dismissals from office. We made some slight change from the British procedure by vesting in the Civil Service Commission the

Dismissals-Mr. Cahan
power of making appointments to office, but the right of dismissal is exclusively vested in the governor in council of Canada.
In Great Britain officials holding office during pleasure may be dismissed by order in council without cause being alleged, but, so far as I have ascertained, every official dismissed from office for an alleged breach of the law is not dismissed until a complaint has been made before a court having jurisdiction in the matter and until that court, after having heard witnesses at a trial, has decided either by judge or by judge and jury that the official has been guilty of a breach of the statutes. That is the complete protection which is afforded by the British procedure and by the constiutional practice of that country.
In Canada officials of the civil service may be dismissed for political partisanship as defined by chapter 22 of the revised statutes of Canada, section 55, which reads as follows:
No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee in the civil service shall be debarred from voting at any Dominion or provincial election if, under the laws governing the said election, he has^ the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with any such election, or contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for any party funds.
2. Any person violating any of the provisions of this section shall he dismissed from the civil service.
Another section provides that the dismissal can be made only by order of the governor in council. This statute, which was introduced into our law in 1918, changed the whole status of the civil service of Canada and should have abolished all other practices with regard to dismissals or recommendations for dismissals which theretofore had obtained in this country. It provides, in brief, that a civil service official may vote if he is entitled to the franchise, but he shall not engage in partisan work in connection with any election; he shall not contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for party funds. Those are the two classes of offences, and the only classes, which constitute political partisanship under our law, in consequence of a breach of which an employee of the civil service may be dismissed. If the governor in council, which is the government of the day, should dismiss an official of the civil service for an alleged act of political partisanship which does not fall within the terms of this provision of the statute, then I suggest that the government itself is responsible for a breach of the law of this country. A mere charge of political partisanship is not sufficient; political partisanship is merely a legal conclusion drawn from certain facts; and in accordance
with British justice-and I may add in accordance with Canadian justice-the complainant is bound to state the specific acts which are alleged to constiute political partisanship, as well as the times when and places where the alleged acts were committed, in order to give the accused full information for the preparation of his defence. Of course, any competent person may lay such a charge, whether he be an ordinary citizen, a member of this house or a member of the government of the country.
I do not wish to use strong terms, but certainly it does outrage our sense of justice and right dealing if the individual who prefers a charge against a civil servant should be permitted to sit as judge and jury and to pass judgment upon his own complaint. Our Canadian law and practice now affords, and should afford, complete protection to an official of the service who has faithfully, competently and efficiently performed- his duty, against any fictitious charge which may be preferred against him. If the minister of a department demands efficient and loyal service from those under his supervision, as he should, then it is necessary that the minister should see that those officials who give such service receive his protection, as minister of the crown, against all fictitious, false or deceitful charges made against them.
If you take the Civil Service Act and read it together with the Inquiries Act you will find that our procedure implies several conditions:	First, the complaint must be made
directly or indirectly to the minister of the crown who has been appointed and solemnly sworn to administer the particular department of government in which the accused is employed; second, it is the bounden duty of that minister of the crown to see to it that his officials, from whom he necessarily demands loyal and efficient service, are completely protected against false and malicious charges or complaints, from whatever source they may emanate; third, except in the case of complete admission or confession of guilt, it is impossible for the minister to fulfil his duty and responsibility in the premises except by ensuring that the accused shall be informed of the nature and details of the charge preferred against him, and that the accused also shall be afforded full opportunity to present his defence and prove himself innocent of the complaint or charge made against him; fourth, to that end it is necessary that the minister, personally or through a commissioner appointed for the purpose, should conduct a full and impartial inquiry into the facts alleged and the issues arising out of such allegations; fifth, our statutes have made

6.	The minister .presiding over any department of the civil service of Canada, may appoint at any time, under the authority of the governor in council, a commissioner or commissioners to investigate and report upon the state and management of the business, or any part of the business, of such department, either in the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service, so far as the same relates to his official duties.
The Inquiries Act vests in the commissioner so appointed very large powers. The commissioner may summon witnesses and require them to give evidence on oath, and he may engage counsel to assist and aid him in such inquiries. However, there are certain matters in which our law allows the commissioner no discretion whatever. The Inquiries Act provides as follows:
12.	The commissioners may allow any person, whose conduct is being investigated under this act, and shall allow any person against whom any charge is made in the course of such investigation, to be represented by counsel.
13.	No report shall be made against any person until reasonable notice shall have been given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him and he shall have been allowed full opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel.
Such are the wise provisions of our laws with respect to inquiries into the alleged misconduct of any officer of any department in our civil service. The accused is allowed to be represented by counsel and reasonable notice shall be given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him. He shall be allowed full opportunity to be heard' in person or by counsel, and the accused is further protected in that even if a report is made against him by the commissioner, in which the minister presiding over that particular department fully concurs, yet the minister may not by his own motion dismiss the accused from his office or employment. The minister can only report the commissioner's findings to the governor in council, and parliament has enacted, for the due protection of the civil servant, a provision that he may be dismissed only by order of the governor in council, that is, by the government of the day upon whom the legal and moral duty and responsibility is placed of assuring to the accused that he has been fully protected in his rights and privileges under the law, including the full opportunity to present his defence and to prove his innocence of the charges of misconduct preferred against him.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house in going fully into the law, but I suggest that it might be considered by the

Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). If an order in council dismissing an official alleges a case which as not true in fact, that official has thb right to proceed to the courts and have the order in oouncil set aside. It is obvious in the case of a civil servant who is receiving a small salary of $1,000 or $1,500 per year that through his very impecuniosity he is denied access to the courts for relief against the order in council affecting his dismissal, where it has been procured by deceit, misrepresentation or through any obvious error.
In the case of Dumoulin, which I have just discussed, I think the action of the minister of the crown was entirely commendable-I know that was the opinion which prevailed throughout the length and breadth of the province from which I come, and in many other provinces-and as a result the civil servants with small salaries and humble positions have a confidence, which they did not have heretofore, in the loyalty to their interests of the chief of their department when they are performing their duties efficiently and honestly. It gave to them a new faith and confidence that justice would prevail in the civil service of Canada whenever the facts were brought to the notice of the minister presiding over any department of the civil service.
It was alleged in that case that an official having been dismissed, his reappointment could not be made because appointments must necessarily emanate from the Civil Service Commission. I have looked into the law in that respect and I differ decidedly from the position which has been taken. The report of the Department of Justice was correct in view of the facts presented to it, as to whether the head of a department could appoint to the civil service a dismissed official, but that is not the real issue. The leal issue was whether or not, when an order in council had been passed under a misapprehension or misrepresentation, or through any other error, the governor in council of itself had the inherent right to amend it3 own order or to rescind its own order which had been obtained through misstatements of facts or other errors. I find that in England and in this country the governor in council has an inherent right to rescind its own order when it has been improperly obtained, or to amend and modify it so that it may express the real facts upon which it is founded, and that inherent right has been exercised time and time again in the history of this country during the last sixty years. Incoming governments have reversed the decisions of their predecessors, and governments, on

ascertainment of the real facts, have rescinded their own orders in council and have modified them and amended them, and that is the modus operandi in which mistakes can be and should be remedied.
This case which I am now approaching appeals to me because the dismissed official had been some fourteen years fulfilling the duties of his office. He has sent to me commendation after commendation from his superior officers approving of the honesty and efficiency and zeal with which he had performed his duty. He was a man of very modest salary; he had children of his own and he had adopted three other children of a brother who was deceased, and had large family responsibilities placed upon him. His being cast on the street at his age and after so many years of service was a misfortune which few of us, who do not live in lowly circumstances, can fully apprehend. For many years I was one of the executive heads of a large construction works employing thousands and even tens of thousands of men. It has been my duty to be at the bedside of many men just as they were passing into eternity from the ravages of a disease or the result of an accident. Contrary to the ordinary view, I never found a man who seemed to be worried very much about his own soul's salvation. What that man was worrying about was his own wife and children in some foreign land, from which he had come to engage in these works, and who were dependent upon his' salary for their well-being. The one thing that he represented to me on his deathbed was: How can my wife and bairns live when I pass out? I have seen other young men from distant lands who seemed to be wild and reckless youths, but who, on their deathbeds, were not concerned about their souls' salvation; each one was wondering how some aged parent, father or mother, in a distant land could survive, if deprived of the contributions which he or she received from his weekly or monthly wage. Therefore I say that dismissals of this kind come home to the families of those dismissed as a cruel misfortune which, if they believe it to be unjust, not only wounds the spirit of the man but wipes out his confidence in the justice of his fello-wmen. It must be admitted that justice is the aim and end of all good government, of all efficient and honest administration in this country. Therefore, on this ground I intend to call your attention to the particular facts of the case of Couture.

Air. Cahan.]
With the permission of the house I would like to put the letter of Mr. Dupre upon Han sard, as I have not the time to read it.
That will be all right.

I then put this letter dated March 13, 1929, from Dupre to Hon. Lucien Cannon, upon Hansard:
Fitzpatrick, Dupre, Gagnon & Parent, Barrister, solicitors, etc.,
Morin Building,
111 Mountain Hill,
Quebec, March 13th, 1929.
Copy.
Honourable Lucien Cannon, K.C.,
Solicitor General,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:-Re: Mr. Charles Hippolyte Couture, Mayor of St. Bernard, county of Dorchester.
As you are aware, Mr. Couture has been dismissed as inspector of weights and measures without any investigation and for supposed political partisanship. Mr. Couture had occupied his position for 14 years.
We are positive that nothing eotdd be found against Mr. Couture even on the ground of political partisanship but in spite of his efforts no investigation has been granted yet. although you have stated in a letter (April 25th, 1928) that you had no objection to such an investigation.
Mr. Couture would like to prove to you and to the public that the grievances against him are illfounded.
You have already before you numerous demands and petitions signed by very prominent persons of the constituency of Dorchester, irrespective of political creeds or opinions, and praying for an investigation.
The reasons alleged, or supposed to be alleged, are that in the course of a meeting, Mr. Couture encouraged some people to manifest against you or your friends. On the other hand. Mr. Couture and his friends emphatically deny such accusations and it is to justify himself and prove the untruth of these accusations that Mr. Couture respectfully prays for an investigation.
Would you have the kindness to grant such an investigation or at least to recommend same.
T apologize for the trouble I am giving you and. with anticipated thanks, I beg you to believe me
Very sincerely yours,

The next letter is dated April 12, 1928, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the Solicitor General. It reads as follows:
Hon. Lucien Cannon,
Solicitor General,
Ottawa.
My dear Colleague:
Relative to your letter of March 16th, Re C. H. Couture, T enclose herewith a memo which I have received from my deputy minister regarding this man.
Will you kindly advise me if you have anything to suggest that I might do further in this matter?
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd) James Malcolm.

Dismissals-Mr. Cahan
A memorandum is enclosed containing the report from the Deputy Minister of Justice, stating that the minister cannot reappoint him.
Did he get back his superannuation money?

He received a cheque and
then went to see the Solicitor General. Believing, as a result of that interview, that he was about to be granted an inquiry he returned the cheque, and I understand that it is now in the possession of the Department of Finance.

He did not cash the
cheque?

No, he did not cash the
cheque, he returned it immediately by return mail. I think I read the letter of April 10, 1929, in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
Will you kindly advise me if you have anything to suggest that I might do further in this matter?
There does not appear to be any reply to that letter in the file.
Hear, hear.

What is the matter
with you?
He is through.

I feel very strongly about
this matter. Whether or not this man is reinstated upon proof of his innocence, he has a right to a public inquiry, as provided for by the Inquiries Act, in order that he may exculpate himself from this charge and vindicate his personal honour as a loyal and efficient servant of the department. I trust the minister will take the same action which his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (.Mr. Euler) took, and follow the precedent then established. I am quite sure that it would not detract from the high reputation which the minister has gained as an honest and efficient administrator of the departmeht which has been placed in his charge by the right hon. the Prime Minister.
In my opening remarks I pointed out that in moving this amendment. I did not desire it to be taken as a vote of want of confidence in the government, but simply to establish what I believe to be an important principle. I trust the right hon. the Prime Minister will accept this amendment. According to the rules of the house, as I pointed out, if this amendment passes it does not defeat a second motion immediately made to go into committee of supply. I refer to section 489 of Beauchesne. I beg to move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart):
That all the words after "that" in the motion of the Honourable the Minister of Finance be struck out and the following words be substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this house no person should be dismissed from his employment in the civil service of Canada on a charge of political partisanship until the allegations of fact, on which such charge is based, shall have been investigated by a commissioner appointed under the provisions of part two of the Inquiries Act, chapter 99 of the revised statutes of Canada, and said commissioner's report thereon shall have been submitted for the consideration of the governor in council."
I submit that is in accordance with the law as it stands, although it may not be quite in accordance with the practice that has grown up. If this resolution were adopted as a matter of policy in the administration of the several departments of government, this would ensure that every man who denies the accusations made against him and who asks for an opportunity of proving his innocence, would have an opportunity to do so, such as the law provides. It would further ensure that the governor in council, in considering these matters which strike at the hearts and homes of so many people, would have the facts before them in passing these orders in council, and in taking the responsibility which every government is bound to assume, of exercising the right of dismissal of officials who have been charged with breaches of the law.

Is the resolution intended
to have a retroactive effect so as to cover the Couture case, or is it only for the future?

The Couture case, I recognize, must now depend upon the discretion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and upon that of the Prime Minister and of his oolleagues. I ask them, and I asked them at the outset, to exercise a discretion in this case in the way that I have suggested, namely, by grabbing an inquiry now, but to provide for the future I ask that we shall obviate difficulties, misfortunes and even possible injustices of this kind by making provision that these civil servants shall have, upon request, the right to an inquiry where they may have an opportunity of proving their innocence, although they are taking a responsibility there that one does not take in a court of justice, where every accused is deemed innocent until proven guilty. Under the English practice an official who is charged with offending against any statute, is dismissed by the government
Dismissals-Mr. Malcolm

only when the complainant has gone into the courts and procured an information or an indiotanent, and a judgment of the court that the man is guilty, so careful are they of preserving the rights and liberties of those employed in their civil service.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal very briefly with this matter as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has reviewed the statements in the case, clearly, concisely and accurately. A member of parliament stated to the minister that he had, not hearsay, but personal knowledge of a civil servani having been actively engaged politically during, not one election, not two, but three elections. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is too clever a lawyer to think that there was any delay in reporting on this man's offence in 1921 or in 1925. Those dates were mentioned purely to show that the man had been, not a late, but a consistent offender. Hon. gentlemen are aware that the practice followed has been a rule which has been accepted by governments for many years and we have no less an authority endorsing the general principle than the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) who, when speaking in the house on April 17 last, admitted that certain dismissals were made o.i his recommendation, which he contended, and which I contend, he had a perfect right to make.	*
That was under an order in council.

Yes. In the case now under consideration the order was granted and the civil servant was dismissed. Everything that could be done to be just and fair to Mr. Couture with regard to his superannuation was done. The matter was discussed with the accountant of the department and a cheque was offered to Mr. Couture. The cheque was later returned, the Department of Justice, when the matter was referred to them, ruled that the governor in council had no authority to reinstate the man. There are two points which I have to consider. My hon. friend says, first, that the dismissal was a reflection on this man's honour. A dismissal for political partisanship is, in my opinion, no reflection on any man's honour or loyalty. It is no reflection except that the man chose to take an interest in party politics and at the same time to act as a civil servant of Canada. A civil servant of Canada has to make the choice between taking an active interest in party politics and
fMr. Cahan.]
holding his job, and I will say to my hon. friend that it is a very good thing for the Dominion of Canada that civil servants have to make that choice. We have evidence in other countries where civil servants are actively engaged in party politics, and I do not think their governments compare favourably with ours. This man's loyalty to the department is unquestioned. I believe Couture was a good public servant, but he apparently did not appreciate his job enough to keep out of politics.
Why not give him an opportunity to prove his case?

Just a moment. I have to choose between the wrord of this man and that of a colleague or any other member of this house, I do not care whether he sits on this side or the other, who says that of his personal knowledge he knows a civil servant to be guilty. I have to choose between two men, and a member of parliament has the right to make a request of the minister.

Does the minister mean
to suggest that if I made a complaint about somebody taking part in politics on behalf of his party, he would dismiss him?

It is the right of every
member to make such a request.
Would the minister dismiss the man?
It has not been the practice in the past to extend such a privilege to the opposition party, but that is the right of a member of parliament.
Has that right existed since 1918, since the Civil Service Act was passed?

It has, and my hon.
friend knows it has been accepted by both parties. It was accepted on April 17 by the leader of the opposition.

Does the minister w'ant the ho.use to understand that if a member on this side makes a charge on his personal responsibility that a civil servant has been guilty of political partisanship, the minister would dismiss him without investigation? That is the gravamen of the- matter.
My hon. friend has the point entirely wrong.
No, I have not.

I say that when a
member of parliament makes a request of the minister for dismissal and states that to his

Dismissals-Mr. Malcolm
personal knowledge the civil servant has taken an active political part in an election, the minister has the right, if he believes the charges to be true, to dismiss without an investigation.
He has the right.
That has been held, and it was held by the leader of the opposition.

I was dealing with the
1911 election before the Civil Service Act was amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The act did not change
anything in that respect.

I am not going to make reference to the dismissals that took place in 1911, although I could refer to many if I chose in my own department. This is the only dismissal that has taken place in the Department of Trade and Commerce since I have taken charge, and I believed that my colleague knew what he was talking about when he said that this man had been consistently guilty of political partisanship. I am not going to deal with the acceptance of the principle of dismissal for political partisanship by citing dismissals in .the past, but I do want to refer to the way in which the matter was handled and which my hon. friend thinks was unfair. No good could have come from an investigation because the man could not be reinstated. The only justice that could be done to him was to give him back his contributions which were payable under the Superannuation Act. I had to choose between the statement of my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who did not say that he made these charges on some evidence of others but that he personally knew of the man's guilt, and Couture's statement. I was not going to open an investigation which could have done Couture no good. It could not have reestablished his honour because his honour was never questioned; his loyalty was never questioned. He simply chose to take part in party politics.

And to violate a statute,
and it is on account of his violating the statute that he is charged with political partisanship.
He does not violate any law of God or man at all.

He was violating section 55
of chapter 22 of the revised statutes of Canada, which constitutes political partisanship, and that is the only ground on which the governor in council had t'be right to dismiss.

That is not the point
I want to discuss. That is not the point, of my hon. friend's criticism at all. My hon. friend takes two grounds for criticism. He says that the whole principle should be changed and that this house should support the principle that when a member lays a complaint an investigation should necessarily follow immediately. I am going to submit to my hon. friend that in some cases complaints may be unjust. In cases in the past civil servants may have been dismissed on very slim charges. Does my hon. friend not think it is better to have our civil servants in Canada keep out of politics. I think the best administration will follow if our civil servants vote as they choose but do not actively engage in an election.
We all agree on that.

That is a principle we
are all agreed on.

Just before the house
rises, may I ask if the minister would bring down at three o'clock the order in council which was agreed upon by Sir W ilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was no order in council.
Yes, I think so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was an
agreement as to the rule, but no order in council.

I think it was embodied
ia writing.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, to review
very briefly the remarks I made before luncheon, I should like to point out to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that I cannot find any orders in council pertaining to dismissals, except one order passed in 1908, which sets out that a complaint against a civil servant of political partisanship shall be made in writing. The Civil Service Act of 190S provides that a civil sea-want may be dismissed for political partisanship. The possible loss of position becomes one of the terms of employment of a civil servant; for he is employed on the understanding that if he engages in promoting the welfare of political parties he is liable to dismissal.
I agree with my hon. friend from St. Law-rence-St. George that Mr. Couture has done nothing for which he can be brought to
Dismissals-Mr. Malcolm

account in a civil or a criminal court, and that no penalty can possibly be imposed upon him. By the terms of his contract of employment he may lose his position due to the fact that the Civil Service Act under which he is employed provides that he may not do certain things. If on investigation the charges were substantiated the dismissal would of course be justified.
Undoubtedly there is an injustice which my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George points out. If the investigation proves that the charges were not of a sufficient serious nature to justify the dismissal, then the government finds itself in the position brought about by the ruling of the Justice department, that under the Civil Service Act it has no power to reinstate that man. He can only again enter the civil service by going through the regular channels prescribed by the Civil Service Commission.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that in this particular case all the requirements of the Civil Service Aot of 1908 have been complied with and the practice followed by all governments since that time has been observed. Complaints of active political partisanship within the personal knowledge of a member of the house had been lodged in writing against an officer of my department. The charge stated that he had been guilty of active political partisanship on three occasions.
I may say that in my opinion it was the only charge which was sufficiently well founded to justify dismissal of an officer of my department since I took office. I took the word of my colleague, a member of the house, when he said that it was on his own personal knowledge that he preferred the charge; that indeed he had been a witness to the man's actions, and therefore knew that he was guilty.
hen Couture asked for an investigation into the charge, I referred the request to the member in question, who plainly said that he saw no reason for an investigation as he had personal knowledge that the man was guilty. In other words. I had either to believe the member of the house who very definitely made the charge, and who is in a position to defend his action, or to take the word of the officer who had been dismissed and whose position had been filled by the Civil Service Commission. Two years afterwards, further representations having been made to him, the member did write the letter read by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George stating that he had no objection to an investigation. But my contention is that no good end could be served by granting the investigation. If I could have reinstated Couture I would have granted his request for an investigation.

Under the law as it stands to-day I can do nothing to put Couture back in his position, because the position has been filled by the Civil Service Commission. There will have to be a change in the act dealing with reinstatement before cases such as this can be dealt with.
In so far as the general principle of my hon. friend's amendment is concerned, I do not hold with it at all. As I have said, it is desirable that civil servants should have the freedom of exercising their franchise, but I think it is undesirable that civil servants should take part in party politics. If we adopt the principle that a minister must hold an investigation every time a member of the house charges that some civil servant has been guilty of an act of political partisanship for any party without leaving to the minister the right to turn down the dozens, yes, hundreds of applications that may come for dismissals, following a general election, then whoever are in charge of the departments will be in a turmoil of investigations, considering dismissals. I contend, no matter what party is in power, that the request must first of all be decided by the minister from the point of view of its seriousness, which will eliminate probably 90 per cent of the charges.

Is not that possible still?
That is quite possible.

My hon. friend agrees
with that point. No minister is anxious to worry himself and the officers of his department with many dismissals; the minor requests he brushes aside. When members of the house, complaining against civil servants for being partisans, are forced to put their charges in writing and forced to say that they know the particular persons have been guilty of an offence which is a violation of the terms of employment they do some thinking before making the charge in writing; and I contend that the regulation in this respect has been of great benefit to the civil servants of Canada. But I do not think that the civil service of Canada will be benefited, or that civil servants will be any more secure in their position against complaints, if we adopt my hon. friend's amendment that, no matter from which member the complaint may come, it will be compulsory on the part of the minister to grant an investigation into the charge that has been brought forward.

I think the resolution calls for such an inquiry only before a dismissal; that is to say, before the governor in council may act, by dismissing the person whom complaint is made against, there shall be a. report from a commissioner Who has inquired into tihe charge.

Dismissals-Mr. Malcolm

If I misinterpreted my
hon. friend's amendment-
That was my intention.
-I will withdraw my argument in that regard; but I understood the amendment to imply that every complaint should call for an investigation.
No, before dismissal, preliminary to dismissal.

So far as that suggestion is concerned, there may be much merit in it. As to whether or not the adoption of that suggestion would involve a want of confidence in the government, I am not prepared to say. I would not support my hon. friend's amendment if it meant a want of confidence in the government.
I did not intend it as a vote of want of confidence.

I shall have to leave it to some of my colleagues to interpret the meaning of the amendment. I was about to say that I should be willing to give the hon. member's suggestion very serious consideration, for I do not think the matter is one that can be settled without consideration.
So far as Couture is concerned, if the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) feels that the charge has not been established I shall have no objection to granting an investigation. I must say however that under the present ruling we cannot restore him to the position which has been filled by another. Should an investigation be held and it is proved that the man's offence was not of such a nature as to justify , his dismissal, all we can do is to try to place him in some other position. To that extent, if my colleague the Solicitor General thinks it advisable, I am prepared to go with my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George.
I understood the minister to say that this is the only case of dismissal in his department since he took charge of it.
Yes.

There were hundreds of
other cases-
I did not say hundreds.

I understood the minister to
say so.
I said that in the administration of departments of government there might be dozens or hundreds of minor [DOT]complaints.
The minister has in mind, I gather, some complaints in his own department.
Quite.
Quite a number of them.
Often.

In what way would those
complaints differ from this one? I understand that in this case the Solicitor General added to his request for dismissal a sentence to the effect that he had personal knowledge of partisanship having been exercised. I should have thought that a written communication from any member of parliament asking for the dismissal of a civil servant on the ground of partisanship would imply personal knowledge on the part of the member; it would imply that the member, before bringing forward the complaint, had personal knowledge of partisanship on the part of the person complained against. Are we to take it that in none of the other cases to which the minister has referred has there been such an indication on the part of the member complaining as to personal knowledge? Is that the distinction?

My hon. friend realizes,
as every hon. member does, that ministers constantly have complaints about civil servants to the effect that they have been engaging in partisan activities, but in a great many cases the evidence is hearsay. Frequently letters are written about men in the civil service; but unless a member of the house complaining is prepared to take responsibility in the matter and to say that he has personal knowledge, I think that ministers as a rule always turn down the consideration of any complaint. And I think it is right that they should.

Perhaps the minister and
I are at cross purposes; I am speaking only of requests for dismissal coming from members-any member at all. I suppose a defeated candidate would be included in that category. I am speaking of them and of them only. Surely a request coming from a member, on his responsibility, for the dismissal of an officer must imply that he has personal knowledge of the matter whereof he complains. There is no hearsay about that. Does the Minister, in referring to many other cases, refer to those cases which have been stated in writing by members, but without the addition of such words as, " I have personal knowledge "? Are those the ones he has turned down?
Dismissals-Mr. Malcolm

My hon. friend is quite
right. Members are inclined probably to make verbal complaints-

I am speaking of written
complaints.
-and verbal complaints are not considered; the order in council of 1923 covered that point.
I am not speatking of them.

So that to-day a complaint must be in writing. If a man writes complaining about a civil servant and says, " I have heard certain things," I do not take such a complaint seriously. If a member is not willing to say he has personal knowledge and is in a position to defend his complaint in the house, I am not prepared to dismiss a civil servant; I am not prepared to take action on hearsay evidence. That is the type of letter to which I pay no attention.

Do I understand the minister to say that any member of this house, whether he be Liberal or Tory or Progressive, may write to the minister to say that he has personal knowledge that such-and-such a civil servant in the department has been engaged in political partisanship, and the minister will thereupon dismiss that civil servant?

Not at all. But the
minister has a right to consider a complaint from any member of the house; that is my interpretation of the custom followed for years.
It would be a defeated government candidate on whose recommendation the minister would act.

A defeated government
candidate would not be a member of the house.
But it is on the recommendation of defeated government candidates that very many dismissals take place.

Not of appointments
under the act.
lion. LUCIEN CANNON (Solicitor General) :	The hon. member for St. Lawrence-
St. George (Mr. Cahan) has brought forward a matter with which I am particularly concerned, and he has broadened out the debate by incorporating in his suggested amendment reforms, complete and entire, in the system which has prevailed in Canada in relation to civil servants guilty of political partisanship, and the means whereby they may be dismissed. At the outset may I say, sir, that [Mr. Geary.)
I do not think it would be possible for this house to accept the amendment of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George otherwise than as meaning that it implies a vote of want of confidence in the government, and in support of the interpretation I would quote Bourinot at page 424:
An amendment moved to the motion to go into committee of supply (or ways and means) does not necessarily involve want of confidence in the administration. When such an amendment simply affirms a general principle, or seta forth a public grievance, and does not directly or impliedly challenge the conduct or policy of the government, it is not. in a parliamentary sense, a motion of want of confidence-
The amendment brought forward by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George implies a challenge of the conduct of the government in connection with this particular matter, and therefore it is a motion of want of confidence,
I do not follow that reasoning.

I think Bourinot's reasoning is very simple. If on the motion to go into supply a member of the house expresses a general principle to which he desires the house to agree, it is not a motion of want of confidence, but if the amendment implies a criticism of the conduct of the government in any particular matter, it then becomes a motion of want of confidence.
Is this not merely the statement of a principle, without any particular application?

I do not like to refuse
to allow my hon. friend to interrupt, but he has spoken for two hours while I have only forty minutes, and I am going to state my case in less than forty minutes if possible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the matter brought up by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is very simple. Many documents have been read; as a matter of fact the entire departmental file has been placed on Hansard, and the purpose for which that file was read is very obvious. Perhaps I might sum up the case and make it very clear and concise so that every hon. member of the house will understand it. A public official in the constituency which I represent had been in the employ of the government for a number of years, and after the elections of 1926, under the practice then existing, as sitting member for the constituency and upon my personal responsibility I wrote the Minister of Trade and Commerce asking for the dismissal of this official on account of partisanship. I do not

Dismissals-Mr. Cannon
withdraw one word of that letter which I wrote to the minister and I do not wish to lessen in any degree the responsibility which I assumed at that time and which I am quite willing to assume before the house and the *country to-day.
The principle at stake is a principle of the very highest order; the dignity of the house itself is concerned in this matter. If the member for a constituency can state from his own personal knowledge that an official or a public .servant of this country has acted in a partisan way, I say with no hesitation at all that if that member of parliament, be he a Tory or a Liberal, wishes to maintain his authority as far as his constituents are concerned, as well as the dignity of the house of which he is a member, there is one duty incumbent upon him to perform; that is, he should see to it that the official is removed from the civil *service. This always has been the rule and the practice, and just here I might recall the expression of opinion given by no less a member of the house than the leader of the opposition. Speaking in this house on April 22 of this year, and not dealing with what might have happened in 1911 but with what did happen last year in one of the western provinces, the leader of the opposition said:
I also recall that the late Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier approved of the general terms of that order.
That was the order in council which gave power to a member of parliament to ask for the dismissal of a civil servant for political partisanship.
Action was taken accordingly, and when last session the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) was able to stand up in this house and say of his own knowledge that he believed a given person to have been guilty of political partisanship, you will recollect, Sir, that at once I said the incident was ended so far as we were concerned.
Those are the words of the leader of the opposition, spoken in this house this year; he said that the moment the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) was in a position to get up in the house and state on his own responsibility that he thought a public official was guilty of political partisanship the matter was ended so far as he and his followers were concerned. Why should the attitude taken by the opposition at that time, expressed by the leader of the opposition, be altered through an amendment brought in this morning by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George? Are there to be two leaders of the opposition? Are there to be two attitudes on the same question? Are we to accept the policy laid down by the leader of the Conservative party in April which I
have just quoted from Hansard, or are we now to adopt a new platform as laid down by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who at times is represented, at least in our papers, as leader of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec?
What are the facts of this case? I wish to say first of all that I have been a candidate in the county of Dorchester in the province of Quebec on nine different occasions; I have won some of my elections and have lost others, and I think if you inquired of my opponents you would find that as a rule I have been a good loser. Although I have represented the county of Dorchester either in the provincial house or in this federal house for the last fifteen years, if the official records of all these departments are looked up it will be found that during the whole of my career I have had only three officials dismissed from the service. I do not believe in political retaliation; when a fight is over I think we should forget the knocks and blows which were exchanged while the battle was on. However, certain cases are exceptional, and as I stated at the outset sometimes the very dignity of the member for the constituency is at stake. In this case my dignity and authority as a member of parliament and a member of the government was at stake.
Couture was appointed shortly after the election of 1911 by the then sitting member who is now a distinguished member of the supreme court of Quebec. Couture had had the inspector of weights and measures dismissed by the member and had taken his place, and the very manner in which he had obtained the situation showed that he was a political partisan. We had two elections in my constituency in 1917 and Couture took a very active part in both; during the election of 1921 he was very active; he was more than active in the election of 1925, but according to the general principle which I had laid down for my guidance as a public man ip my constituency of Dorchester, I did not ask for his dismissal. When I was holding a public meeting in the parish of St. Bernard in 1927, the parish where Couture lives, I had great difficulty in being heard. I think a member who has sat for a constituency can ask at least that his electors give him the privilege of being heard. What was the cause of the disturbance? The cause was a group of children on Couture's property, and Couture himself standing only a few feet away. That disturbance lasted for over half an hour and he never took any steps to stop it, nor did he do the least thing to allow me to be freely heard.
Dismissals-Mr. Cannon
What a serious charge.

I ask any member of this house, whether he sits on this side or on the other side, if he were attending a public meeting and a disturbance was being carried on, would he not in all fairness see that a proper hearing was given, not only to the candidate during the election but to the former member who had represented the constituency for several years? A few days after this meeting my opponent conducted a meeting in the parish-I do not wish to reopen the questions which were settled on polling day, because they were numerous and serious and could occupy the attention of any serious audience-and he took it upon himself to make a personal attack against myself. I would have been perfectly willing to allow that to pass, but a personal attack was made against my family, against my wife and against my children; Couture was present at that meeting and gave encouragement to the speaker.
In what way? '

If a member, no matter to what party he belongs, cannot have the right of being respected by public officials, it is about time that we closed the doors of this House of Commons and allowed someone else to handle the public business of Canada.
That is my stand in this matter. When those happenings occurred I publicly told Couture that if my party came back into power I would see that he was fired, and I have kept my promise. There are many Conservatives in the public service in the county of Dorchester, and I recognize and acknowledge their right of voting whichever way they desire, as long as they perform their duties as public officials to their own credit and to the benefit of our country. As long as I am a member of this house, I will not stand for any public official insulting either the sitting member or the candidate in any election.
If the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George desires to introduce a new principle, is he willing to make it retroactive? I have been the object of discussion to-day in the
House of Commons because of one dismissal in my county made under the circumstances I have just described. If I wanted to play politics in this matter I would ask the hon. gentleman to take cognizance of the list of those who were dismissed in the county of Dorchester in the year 1911 when there was a change in government.
Read it.
It is too long, I do not wish to delay the house.
Put it on Hansard.
I have a list of twenty-seven postmasters who were dismissed in 191112 by the then sitting member.

Not rural delivery postmasters. There was no investigation although the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was then in active politics.

eleven.

I am coming now to what the hon. gentleman described this morning as the deathbed scene, and the terrible condition in which Couture's family might have been placed. I will say to the hon. member that it was no pleasure to me to have to take the action which I did take, but I took it because I thought I had not only the right to do so but a duty to perform.
You took that action because of what took place at a meeting at which you were not present and of which you had no personal knowledge, according to your own statement.

In 1911, in the very department that we are discussing now, inspector of weights and measures Mr. Bugeaud was dismissed for political partisanship in December of that j'ear. What about his family? What about the inquiry that the bon. gentleman is asking for? Mr. Guay was dismissed on January 1, 1912; Mr. Caldwell was dismissed on August 1, 1913, and Mr. Prefontaine was dismissed on October 1, 1913. These are four dismissals in the one office in Quebec, and Mr. Couture, whom the hon. gentleman has taken under his wing to-day, replaced one of those who had been dismissed.
The larger question remains: should this be changed? Some years ago it was proposed in France that the death penalty be abolished, and the president answered by saying: "Que messieurs les assassins commeneent." "Let the murderers give an example first." In 1911, 12,000 Liberal employees were dismissed without any inquiry. Will the hon. gentleman consent to make his amendment retroactive and allow those 12,000 employees to have an inquiry? That is a fair question. That is a fair way of putting the matter. Would the

lion, gentleman allow his amendment to be retroactive in order that the twenty-seven postmasters in my constituency whose names were mentioned, be given an inquiry and reinstatement?
Certainly I would if any one of them ever asked for an inquiry and it was refused.

I am perfectly willing to
accept the hon. gentleman's answer provided it is confirmed by his leader, because, as I stated at the outset, the attitude of the two hon. gentlemen on this matter is quite divergent. The leader of the opposition said that the right thing to do when a man is guilty of partisanship is to dismiss him.
I did not say that.

I quoted from Hansard
what my hon. friend said.
I said: When the member says so of his personal knowledge.
This is my case.

The minister was not at
the meeting.
At what meeting?
At the meeting of Mr. Cote of which the minister complains.
I am complaining of both meetings, the one where I addressed the electors and the one where Cote was.

And the minister was not
present at Mr. Cote's meeting.
I hope the hon. gentleman will be reasonable enough to admit that I know more about what took place in my constituency in 1926 than he did when he was in Montreal.
Quite so.

The hon. gentleman makes a strong argument that Couture says that he should not have been dismissed. Has anyone ever heard of an official who was dismissed claiming that he was rightly so? I have not. To end this incident of a very minor character which has taken up already too much af the time of the house, because I have done }nly in one instance what other members have lone in many where their names have never been mentioned, let me say this: there has

been one case in my constituency. As to the larger issue whether the whole procedure should be changed, this is a matter of very serious policy which I leave to the opinion of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few
words to say on this matter. I have heard the two-hour speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). If he goes to the Calgary stampede this year and meets some Indians there, they will probably call him "Chief Long Breath." The last issue of Life says that besides dance marathons, there might be chewing gum and teeth-brushing endurance contests. Why not have a speech marathon, not for the future, but with a retroactive effect? In this case, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George would be an easy winner, not with his two-hour speech of to-day but with the six-hour speech he delivered two years ago. In France and in England an hon. member would be covered with ridicule if he spoke for two hours on a single case in regard 'to which he did not know the real facts.
When the Tories were in power, the people who were dismissed were as numerous as the stars of the sky and the sands of the desert. Now the Tories complain and when their friends make trouble during an election, they would like to have them promoted instead of dismissed. I am in favour of the freedom of the franchise for all the employrees in the public service; whether they are Tories, Grits, socialists or anything else, they should be entitled to enjoy their franchise with the greatest freedom. But when it comes to canvassing and making trouble at meetings, that is entirely different. I can speak freely on this subject because I have not asked for many dismissals in my constituency. There are some Tories amongst the civil servants in my constituency, but I do not bother about them. They can vote as they like. But if they cause trouble in meetings, they should be told that they cannot long retain their positions. I think this would be a good opportunity to inform all employees in the civil service to-day that if they want to make trouble during elections or at other times by canvassing against the candidates whoever they may be, they run the risk of being dismissed.
I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr Malcolm) and the Solicitor General (Mr Cannon) on their clear expose of the case.
Amendment (Mr. Cahan) negatived on division.

Fish Traps-Mr. Neill
['Certainly.']

I
understand that this motion covers the estimates, not only of the Department of Trade and Commerce but of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and therefore I should like to say a few words in connection with a subject that comes under the latter department. I am rather timid about introducing this, or, indeed, any subject in the house; I aim afraid of adding to that terrible reputation which was ascribed <to me yesterday, I see, by reading Hansard. I read it in Hansard because I did not hear a word of it at the time it was uttered. I have no objection to those sentiments being uttered in the house; they are his sentiments, not mine. Indeed, I read them with a certain amount of sympathy, because I recognized them as being the emanation of what I myself sometimes suffer from, namely, an over-quick temper and a bilious disposition. I have striven to be more successful than he, and I think I really have been, in concealing my mean disposition in that regard. I have remembered the doctrine put forward by Solomon. "H'e that ruleth his spirit is greater than he tihat taketh a city." I think I can stake my reputation for courtesy in this house up against that of the hon. leader, who gave me such a terrible reputation. Mr. Speaker, human nature is a curious thing-I am speaking generally now. Some men remind one of sausages. They are very thinskinned, smooth on the outside, but you never know how much of the real hog is in them until you get under their skin.
I wish to make a mild protest in connection with another matter, and that is the habit some hon. members have dropped into, unintentionally I believe, when they are making some remarks, perhaps a bit of biting criticism or an offensive remark about some other member, of speaking in so low a tone that while the remark is audible to the reporter and to the few members sitting around, it is not audible to the member to whom it is applied, and consequently he has no opportunity either to hear or to reply to it. I am quite sure that this is so opposed to any idea of courtesy or courage that I need only to mention it for hon. members to be more careful in the future in that regard.
As regards the Department of Marine and Fisheries, I want to bring up a matter in connection with fish traps. I should like briefly to outline the situation. On the 7th of April last I addressed the following letter to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries: 78594-208
The Hon. P. J. A. Cardin,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear sir:
In Vancouver province just to hand I see notice that Judge Ellis has been appointed by you to inquire whether fish traps for salmon should be permitted in northern British Columbia.	_
I have heard rumours of this, but took it for granted that as I represent so many of the fishing interest of British Columbia, that 1 would have been given an opportunity of being heard before such a drastic step was taken.
I understood that for some years past, it has been the settled policy of this government not to allow traps in northern waters. Such has been repeatedly announced as the policy and has been carried out. Why then change it without notice, or at least give opportunity of changing it?
I think the step is bad policy, and equally bad politics. The policy has been carried out for some yeaTs. I have heard no demand for a change.
Is it permitted me to ask if there was any demand for a change, from whence did it emanate? Did any boards of trade, organizations of fishermen or of cannery men, ask for it?
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) A. W. Neill.
That was on April 7th, and I have not yet had a reply. On May 14th I brought the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister, on the orders of the day. I briefly stated the situation and asked if there might be an opportunity given for discussion of the matter in this house. I was promised a reply later, but I have not yet had one. Under date of May 31st, last Friday, I brought the matter up again in the house and said that I proposed to discuss the matter on the Marine and Fisheries estimates, and in order to be in a position to do so intelligently I asked if the report of the commissioner who had been appointed, and whose investigation at that time had certainly been completed, would be laid on the table for our guidance in the debate. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries replied as follows:
I shall do the best I can to meet the request of my hon. friend.
The report so far as I know has not yet been laid on the table; if it has been, I am ignorant of it. The estimates will soon be coming up and that is the only opportunity we shall have this session of discussing the matter. I again ask if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will not lay this report on the table. I have a telegram from British Columbia to the effect that that report was mailed eight or nine days ago, so it must be in the possession of the government now. I do not want to discuss the matter at this



Supply-Trade and Commerce
stage, and I am mentioning it only that we may have the report before us when the estimates are being considered, and I would ask that some at least of the estimates be held over until we have had an opportunity to consider the report, and then we can discuss the matter intelligently. This is a matter of very considerable importance to a large number of people in British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: I have no objection at all to undertaking to comply with the request of my hon. friend.
When? Will it be to-day?
Yes.

Thank you.
