The house in committee of supply, Mr. Laflamme in the chair.
Trade and Commerce-British and foreign news service, $32,000.
Would the minister give a brief explanation?

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: This is a grant made to Reuter's news service for distributing Canadian news items in all parts of Great Britain and in foreign countries. The service has been in existence for several years. The total number of news items pertaining to Canada distributed in 1928 was 7,335. Reuter's are distributing news items to a group of British papers, sixty-three in number, carrying out the terms of the agreement by which items of Canadian news are distributed throughout Great Britain and foreign countries. We find that this method is more economical than any other.

Has the amount been
the same for a number of years?
Yes.
Was not this item cut in half a couple of years ago, and increased again last year?
Yes, the item was in the main estimates and increased in the supplemental.
Does the minister consider that we are getting good value for the expenditure of this $32,000?

I can assure my hon. friend that we are getting very good value for it. In 1927-28 we had 13,571 news items regarding Canada wired 'by Reuter's to different papers in different countries of the world. The figure I gave a moment ago of 7,335 news items distributed in 1928 covers only three-quarters of the year. I do not want to weary the committee with a summary of the papers to which Reuter's distribute news items, but I can assure my hon. friend that in the opinion of my department we are getting a very good service.

Item agreed to.
Commercial intelligence service, including miscellaneous expenditure in connection with the development and extension of Canada's trade, $750,000.
The minister might give us some explanation.

This is an increase of $250,000 and is due to the opening of three new trade commissioners' offices and the necessary staffs in connection therewith, and to the contemplated opening of six new trade commissioners' offices and the embarking on a much wider program with a view to expansion of the activities of the department.
Where are the offices?
Chicago and San Francisco, Oslo, Hong Kong and Havana.
What does the minister expect to gain from an office in Chicago?

They will sell us more
goods.

I cannot make any
definite pronouncement to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) as to what business may result from contact with the Chicago market, but it is felt that there is a very great market in Chicago for certain Canadian products, just as there is in New York.
If they will let you into that market.

It was decided to open up trade offices in Chicago and San Francisco to allow Canadian shippers interested to get in closer touch there than they could through the New York office.
32S1

Svpply-Trade and Commerce

I quite understand the desirability of making reasonable efforts to get into the Chicago market-if the Americans wish us to go there. The trouble is that they do not wish us to go there. Why should we spend money in Chicago when we know that there is not the slightest chance of selling them our goods?

I think my hon. friend has had enough experience of the Department of Trade and Commerce to know that our office in New York is of very great service m keeping our shippers in touch with foreign buyers who are visiting that city. I do not think our trade commissioner in Chicago will do any less valuable work than has been done in New York. Many Canadian business men are strongly of the opinion that trade offices in Chicago and San Francisco would give just the same excellent results as have followed the establishment of our trade office in New York. A great many oriental buyers go to San Francisco. We feel that we would be doing a good stroke of business by establishing a trade office there to get in touch with buyers who might be induced to come to Canada. The same remarks apply to Chicago.

The minister is too good
a business man to expect to "put that over." People who want to sell goods go to the place where the market is; they do not depend on an outside competitor to provide them with the market.
Do those offices do anything in connection with the sale of cereals and other agricultural products?
Yes.

Will the minister name
me a single officer of the Department of Trade and Commerce who did anything last year in connection with the sale of wheat?

I think my hon. friend
is quite right in regard to that, because in so far as the sale of wheat is concerned it is usually sold on contract, and I do not think a trade commissioner could be of very much assistance in that regard or in the sale of newsprint. I may tell my hon. friend from Lincoln that a few days ago a Canadian business man reported to us that, although the Chicago office has been open only two weeks, when he called there he found fourteen men waiting to make inquiries of our commissioner with regard to the market for Canadian commodities which they wanted to sell.

To sell to us?
78594-208i
No; these men were trying to sell their commodities in Chicago, and were asking for assistance from our trade commissioner.
Could the minister tell us one thing they ever sold?

I think my hon. friend
is a little unfair. The office has been opened only two weeks. I am quite frank to say that the experiment looks advisable to me. If it does not prove so, and the commissioner at that point cannot show that he has been benefiting the Canadian shipper, then I think the opening of the office is subject to criticism.

Surely, the minister will
find it very hard to prove that the trade commissioner succeeds in doing anything on behalf of Canadian shippers. How can he Show us that the trade commissioner could do anything?

My hon. Mend knows
that these offices can show what sale3 they make. My deputy has just handed me a memorandum from the director of commercial intelligence stating that one outstanding example of the year's work, so far as the alertness on the part of our trade commissioners is concerned, was reported by one of the firms who benefited. This 'has to do with an agricultural product-apples.	Our trade commissioner at Brussels discovered in November that there was going to be a very excellent opportunity for the sale of Canadian apples. He took the matter up with Mr. Forsyth Smith, the trade commissioner at Liverpool. Mr. Smith notified the Department of Agriculture here, who got in touch with the shippers of apples in the maritime provinces, and for the first time in history, through the activity of these men, we have shipped 85,000 ban-els of apples this year to Belgium, valued at $467,000. That market had apparently been left in abeyance until the trade commissioner saw its possibilities and informed our shippers. I think my hon. friend realizes that from time to time we get many letters of appreciation of the -work done by our trade commissioners. I admit that the work which passes through these offices cannot be tabulated, because much depends on the energy of the man selling his goods, his prices, tariffs and other considerations; but that our trade commissioners are of great assistance to Canadian shippers can be borne out by the letters we receive from the shippers themselves.

When the minister is
asked a question about Chicago, he switches over to Brussels. He puts me in mind of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
another minister who was instrumental a few years ago in making a treaty with Belgium. He told us in the same flowing language about the enormous quantities of butter the treaty would enable our dairymen to sell to Belgium. "Why," he said, "already contracts have been made in Montreal." But that butter never got into our export returns; it melted somewhere. At the same time the Minister of Justice said:	"We are not making this treaty
for the old habitants of Jacques Cartier's time, we are making it for the present day farmers of Quebec." I reminded him at the time that the old people who have been dead two hundred years sold just as much butter to Belgium as do their present day successors. The Minister of Trade and Commerce follows the same line-now he tells us about apples. I do not object to making an arrangement through our trade commissioners with people who want to trade with us. But what is the use of making trade arrangements with people Who put their tariff up so high that we cannot ell to them. I do object to.spending money in a country whose people say deliberately they will not trrde with us, that they will put up their tariff so high that it will effectively exclude our products from their market. That is what has hapened in France, and I told the minister a few years ago what would happen there. We enter into a treaty with them, giving them a fixed rate of duty, and we allow them to impose against us a rate of duty variable from day to day. They have changed their rate of duty so that our trade has vanished, and now I understand that wheat, although we made a treaty with them by which we got a minimum tariff, has now gone up, and is going up still further. And it will continue to do so without our being able to do a thing, because we have a stationary tariff.

Before the minister replies to the hon. member I want to make one or two observations. In his last remarks the minister had something to say about letters he had received from Canadian shippers. I should like him to say a word or two with reference to the letters that he is receiving from shippers who are largely in Europe and abroad. I venture the opinion that never in the history of the Department of Trade and Commerce has there been so much correspondence from manufacturers who find their domicile on the European continent; and at the same time the statistics will show that we are presently receiving from our good neighbour to the south more in the line of manufactured goods than perhaps at any other time in the history of this Domin-

ion. In that same connection I want to point out that a situation has arisen in Canada-the statistics will prove it-which is going to be very embarrassing for this country as one year succeeds another. It is this: the general average of prices in the United States to-day, on commodities made from raw materials which are abundant in this country, is on a level of 10 to 20 per cent higher than are the selling prices of manufactured goods from these raw materials which are enjoyed in this Dominion. This situation arises: immediately there is a small shortage of raw material in that great consuming country of 110,000,000 people, we find that the manufacturers over there come to Canada and take away from the manufacturers of this country their source of raw materials; if they do not take away the raw materials they so enhance the price of raw materials to the manufacturers of this country that one by one those manufacturers find themselves no longer in the position of manufacturers but rather of dealers in perhaps the same finished commodities, buying those finished commodities on the European continent and bringing them here to hold their trade.
The minister in his last words told this house that he was well pleased with the letters he was receiving from shippers in this country. I want him in fairness to the house to make a few observations with regard to the letters he is receiving from the shippers in other lands. To enlarge the point a little further; it is a well know fact that the duty against commodities coming in from the European continent is not nearly so high coming into Canada as that duty is against these European manufacturers going into the United States. The result is that those engaged in industry find that their market price is set by the market price which the shippers in Europe are able to make. The market price for a large part of our commodities is set, not perhaps so much in London and Liverpool, as in days gone by, but in Hamburg, Paris, Lyons, Brussels, Antwerp and Rotterdam. They cannot get their goods into the United States. I hesitate to make the statement- the minister no doubt will enlarge the point for us-but I venture the opinion that they dump those goods into Canada, so that the manufacturer who is trying to make a livelihood in this country finds himself on the one hand deprived of the raw material for the manufacture of his goods, by reason of the fact that the general level of prices in the United States for the finished commodities is a little higher than it is in Canada-finds himself, I say, deprived of that raw material -and at the same time finds his market

Supply-Trade and Commerce
flooded by finished material produced in Europe and Great Britain. I would ask that the minister be good enough to see to it that every possible protection that is given to us in the statutes as they exist is taken advantage of, so that in the final analysis we shall not remain between the upper and the nether millstones in the matter of industry in this country.
I had the pleasure last year of directing to the minister's attention another point, and I hope that when he makes his reply he will tell us what is being done in that connection. That particular point, hon. gentlemen will remember, had something to do with this fact. Europeans find themselves able to enter their goods into Great Britain free of duty. Great Britain, on the other hand, finds herself able to ship goods to Canada under the British preference. We are glad to have the British preference, but we desire that those who are shipping into this country under that preference shall play fair. We do not want them to ship their commodities into this country under a preference and at the same time, in the same month, replenish their own supply, for their own consumption, from Europe, using the British preference just for the sole purpose of being able to manufacture over there and ship goods into Canada. We do not want them to ship goods under the preferential tariff and at the same time supply their home market with goods manufactured in Europe under conditions such as every hon. member knows exist on the continent. If this process continues, it is not too much to say that it is only a matter of time when we shall find in Canada that our standard of living, of which we make such a boast and are rightly so proud, will deteriorate to the standard of living under which those people in Europe are living to-day, and to which we do not like to refer. I should like the minister to enlarge on these two or three phases of the present trade situation and to give to the committee some idea of what is being done to look after the interests of those people in our midst who are employed in Canadian industry.

In reply to my hon. friend, who objected strongly to the opening of an office in Chicago, on the ground that we should not establish an office in a country whose tariff was unfavourable to the entry of Canadian goods, I can only say that I should not care to take the stand that we ought not to try to sell our goods to anyone who will buy them. I should not like to take the stand, that because the United States decided to raise their tariff on two
or three items we should step out of the market and say we cannot do anything. Canadian business men have represented to the department the advisability of this country having offices in Chicago. Whether or not those offices are going to be very helpful I will not venture to prophesy, but I think they will. I do think that until it is shown that the offices have not been helpful, it cannot be argued that they should not be established. I fully admit what my hon. friend says; the United States so frames its tariffs as to make it very difficult for us to trade with that country. But that we do trade with the United States the hon. member does not deny; he does not deny that we send many commodities to the country to the south of us. I will not bother to give the list.

Three-fifths consists of
wood and wood products.

A good deal of it, yes.
With regard to the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) with reference to assistance in the sale of wheat, I may say that only on one or two occasions have our men found themselves able to be of much assistance in this direction. Last year in Mexico, our commissioner, Mr. Wilde, did endeavour to be of assistance to Canadian shippers in a general way by getting some of the Mexican buyers to take Canadian wheat. He succeeded in selling in the year about $300,000 worth. I happen to have his report on the matter before me. Our men in Italy at present are making a survey to assist in getting Italy to buy more of our hard durum wheat, which was under discussion the other day.
They have placed a duty of 75 cents a bushel on that wheat.

I quite appreciate that
fact, if that be true, it will be harder for our men, but still because we have duties against us I cannot hold that we should give up the work of trying to promote trade through, our comercial intelligence service, which was started many years ago and which has been carried on under many governments. I believe Canadian exporters are of the opinion that the service has been of vast assistance to them, and I think it can be made of more assistance. As a matter of fact I am free to say, without desiring to criticize my colleagues, that I do not think we are more than scratching the surface in the way of giving assistance to the business men of Canada through commercial intelligence. I believe a very great

Supply-Trade and Commerce
deal more help can be given than has been given, and if I were on the opposite side of the house and one of my hon. friends were minister I would be likely to criticize him for not opening more trade offices.

It depends where they
are opened.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend that there is not much use in opening offices in places where it is difficult to do business, but I do not admit that because it is difficult we should not try to do business. I do not think we should take everything lying down.
Hear, hear.
I do not think we should refuse to go into the markets of the United States; as far as I am concerned I am just as anxious to sell there as anywhere else-

We have not a trade
office at Geneva, have we?

That is a diplomatic
office to which my hon. friend is referring; of course, he is a lawyer and he knows more about diplomacy.

The minister made a
reference to hard durum wheat. Will he be good enough to explain what he means by a hard durum wheat?

Durum wheat is a very
hard, flinty wheat, as my hon. friend probably knows better than I do.
A macaroni wheat.

Yes. The word "durum" is a trade name for this particular wheat, which is largely grown in Manitoba. It does not grade in with our red spring wheat at all; it does not mill the same and the flour millers do not use it. It has found its outlet in the macaroni mills on the continent, and according to my information it cannot be mixed with our red spring wheat because of the difference in texture. It is not sold on the exchanges to the extent spring wheat is sold; it is disposed of in smaller parcels and there is a smaller quantity grown.

I would like to ask a
question in regard to the markets for wheat. I have been informed by people in the grain trade that practically all the wheat for European consumption is bought by a single firm in Liverpool; I am told that one house in Liverpool buys for fifteen European countries. Can the minister tell me whether or not that is correct?
IMr. Malcolm.]
I believe that statement is rather exaggerated.

Among the countries
named by my informant were France and Italy, and I recall an incident which took place ait the beginning of the session, when the Minister of Finance informed the house that the trade figures did not correctly represent the trade between Canada and France, because he had found that some wheat consigned to Great Britain had eventually reached France. My informant tells me that this wheat was bought by a firm in Britain and the destination changed to France while the wheat was on the Atlantic. It was really an export from Canada to Great Britain; the profit was made in Great Britain, and it wa3 not an export to France at all. Great Britain exported that grain to France.
I think that is true.

And I am told that the
firm which bought that grain for France buys all the grain for Italy and thirteen other countries as well. I am to'ld that there is no competition at all in the purchasing of grain at Liverpool because this one house controls the situation and buys for practically all the European countries which import grain. If that is so I -can understand the lack of competition, and perhaps that is reflected in the price offered.

I hardly think that statement is absolutely correct. The pool has some selling offices on the continent, and they are extending those offices; at the moment they are discussing opening an office in Milan, and in fact we have been asked to make some inquiries for them in that regard. They now have an agent in Milan and also have some agents in France. I do not want to labour the point raised by my hon. friend with regard to the crediting of exports to Great Britain, but I think hon. members generally realize that there is a difficulty in compiling consumption figures as against actual trade figures. We do not know whether all the newsprint we sent to the United States actually remains in that country; they may reexport small quantities of it.

Yes, but in that case we export directly to the United States, while in regard to the grain the export was made to Great Britain and the Minister of Finance tried to switch it to show that it was really an export to France.

It would be an export
to France if the grain left Montreal, as is often

the case, consigned to a Liverpool broker who bought it for delivery with the option of more than one point of destination. The grain might be diverted to France or to Belgium.

But the export was to
Great Britain.

It would be a sale to
Great Britain, but the consumption figure would be shown by France. I think my hon. friend will agree with that.
I think it is artificial.

France and Belgium
both keep their figures according to the country ' of origin; this would be shown as Canadian grain, while we show it as a sale to Great Britain.
The object of the Minister of Finance was to give a favourable impression with regard to our trade with France under his treaty.
I quite appreciate that.

I understood the minister
to say he was opening a trade office in Chicago. What class of goods will Chicago probably buy from us?

Is it proposed to open
any other offices in the United States in addition to the one at Chicago?

No. I cannot tell my hon. friend what commodities we might sell in Chicago but I can give him a few items as to trade which has been the direct result of the work of our New York office this year. That office has been responsible for the sale of lumber to the extent of $3,750, for the sale of canned salmon to the extent of $-1,800,000. They have also made some direct sales of Canadian cattle and there is a trade developing between Canada and the United States in certain varieties of biscuits, although this year that trade amounted to only $158,000.

May I take it that these
trade commissioners will be experts in appraising the values of the different goods sold in the different countries of the world1? Last year two appraisers were appointed for cities in Germany, and I want to ask the minister if the knowledge obtained by these commissioners with regard to the values of different goods will be available to us?

I am sorry; I did not
quite understand my hon. friend's question.

Will the knowledge and
information obtained by these commissioners in the different countries, with regard to the values of different commodities, be available
to us?

I can assure my hon.
friend that we have the statistics here with regard to most foreign countries, but I do not know which commodity he would like inquired into.
Anything we have to sell.

I think my hon. friend
realizes that the very duty of a trade commissioner in a foreign country is to survey the field and, if he finds any opportunity for trade, to forward that information here. It is distributed from the commercial intelligence office here to the various exporters, or the trade commissioner may communicate' direct with the Canadian industrialist who is likely to be able to fill the orders the trade commissioner believes can be obtained. His job is to study the market in order to help the Canadian exporter.
Does he take the orders?

I can assure the hon.
member that he comes mighty close to it.

At times he comes too
close.
He gives every assistance to Canadian firms.

Does he assist the live
stock business in any way?

Yes, I think every branch of industry is referred to our trade commissioners for information as to available markets. After all is said and done, I think my hon. friend realizes that the question asked by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) is rather a pertinent one. The hon. member asked if he actually took the orders. That is not his duty. His duty is to assist Canadian exporters in every way 'he can; find information for them and help them to establish connections and agencies. Since the commercial intelligence department was started years ago, I do not think it can be said that any Canadian exporter has received anything but a courteous answer and the utmost assistance when he made inquiries of our offices abroad.

How many countries import wheat from us and how many countries import our flour?

Every European country

That is possibly correct.
Are we encouraging the exportation of wheat as against the exportation of flour; how is it that we are able to send our flour to so many countries and our wheat to so few?
I think the hon. member must realize that every country in the world does not grind wheat.
With reference to the exportation of wheat, I would advise the committee that the pool have agencies both in France and Italy.

They have an agent in
Italy, not an agency.

I congratulate the minister upon opening more trade agencies in the United States, as I think we have waited too long to do this. Although the American tariff is agaiuist us, if the United States manufacturer takes full advantage of that tariff there is no reason why our goods should not go over the tariff wall. Would the minister advise the committee of the number of trade agencies which we have and where they are located?

We have offices in Melbourne, Australia; London; Calcutta; Glasgow; Hamburg; Liverpool; Paris; Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro on the east coast of South America; Lima on the west coast of South America; New York; Bristol; Milan; Mexico City; Havana; Shanghai; Auckland; Kobe; Batavia; Kingston; Jamaica; Brussels; Rotterdam; Pert of Spain; Dublin and Cape Town. The new offices will be located at Hong Kong; Panama; Oslo; Athens; Chicago and San Francisco.
Could the minister advise the committee how many trade agents or commissioners the United States have in Canada?
I am sorry but I cannot give the hon. member that information.
They call them commercial agencies.

Would the department
have that information?
fMr. Kaiser.]

It can be secured for
the hon. member if he desires it. I think they are called trade commissioners, but I do not know how many offices are established in Canada.

They have one here in
Ottawa.

Would the minister be
good enough to answer the questions I asked?
I thought the hon. member was making a speech, and I did not get the import of his questions.

If the minister wants a
speech we can oblige him any time he is ready. I asked the minister to make some observations to the house with regard to the amount of service which is being given to importers to this country who are bringing European and other goods to Canada and supplying a demand which could very readily be supplied by our own home industries.

The whole object of our commercial intelligence department is to assist Canadians who desire to export; it has nothing whatever to do with the importing of goods. Our trade commissioners do not assist Canadian merchants to find commodities; that is not their job. The trade commissioner's job is to help the Canadian exporter find a market. I hope the hon. member does not think that the work of the Canadian commercial intelligence department has been based on the principle of helping to buy foreign goods? It is based on the principle of selling Canadian goods abroad. [DOT]

But they are wandering
into the other line of endeavour.
Oh, no.

My next question had to
do with the commodities from Europe finding their way into Great Britain and replacing consumption there, and Great Britain in turn exporting them to Canada under the British preference. I asked this same question last year and perhaps the minister has had a chance to think it over and may be able to give me a reply this year?

I do not think the hon. member is fair in asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he is putting through estimates on commercial intelligence, to go into a question which belongs properly to the Minister of National Revenue.
Or National Defence.

Perhaps. As to the
hon. member's suggestion that commodities of continental manufacture might come via

Great Britain and enter Canada under the British preferential tariff, I think he must recall the discussion which took place a short time ago in the house, when the Minister of National Revenue was discussing the enactment of the 50 per cent British labour content requirement. That matter comes purely within the jurisdiction of the Department of National Revenue and this vote has nothing whatever to do with it.

The third question had to
do with the export from this country of raw material. Are our trade commissioners finding markets for this raw material? Would the minister give the committee some information with regard to how the work of the offices would be divided up as between raw materials and manufactured goods? In other words, how much emphasis has the minister given in his instructions to these trade commissioners as to the service they should give in connection with t'he sale of raw materials as against manufactured goods?

The work of the Canadian trade commissioner is the same as that of any other public servant, he is Supposed to be of assistance to Canadian exporters. A Canadian exporter may desire to export newsprint and may ask for a survey. A Canadian exporter may desire to . export wood pulp and he may ask the trade commissioner to secure for him some information as to possible markets for that commodity. He may ask the commissioner to find a market for pulpwood. I am giving these illustrations advisedly, because any man who believes in eihployment in this country knows that it is better to export newsprint than to export wood pulp, and it is better to export wood pulp than to export pulpwood. I hope t'he hon. member does not think that the trade commissioner has it within his jurisdiction to dictate to the exporter and say to him that he is not doing the right thing when he does not grind his pulpwood up and sell it in the . form of paper. These men are employed for the service of Canadian exporters, no matter what their line of business may be. I can quite conceive that my hon. friend might say that we should not ship any finished leather to New York, but if we can ship leather and cannot ship shoes, why not rfiip leather? I do not think it is within the province of the trade commissioners to dictate; it is their duty to serve. The commercial intelligence branch is a service branch for which this house votes money. It gathers information which it is difficult for business firms to obtain in foreign countries, and
supplies the information to Canadian exporters. It is not a department which should dictate governmental policy. It has to do the best it can under whatever policy may be in effect.

Surely the minister must
admit that they have direction. He does not want to leave with the house the impression that they are merely employed on surveys for some of the Canadian exporters. * Have they enough business from Canadian exporters to keep them employed 100 per cent of their time? There must be some portion of their time when they are looking for something to do, and when they receive direction from the minister as to what sort of service they are going to render. Will the minister tell us what these trade commissioners are doing during the portion of their time that they must find on their hands when they are not making a particular survey for some exporter of some particular commodity? There must be some guiding policy given by the minister, and surely we have a right to know what surveys are being made and what they consist of.

The trade commissioners representing Canada do not waste much time. We have some extremely good men in the service. As regards their not having direction,
I do not think the trade commissioners ever had any better direction than they have today under Mr. Chester Payne, the director of the commercial intelligence service. My hon. friend would like some information. May I read the progress reports of the office in Buenos Aires giving new business secured for Canadian firms directly by the office amounting to $164,888.
For how long a period?

This is the new business secured during the year. Newsprint sold through the office by the efforts of Commissioner McCoH amounted to $40,000. He sold $31,000 worth of radio supplies. Elastic webb, which is another article that we have been able to introduce into the Argentine, was sold to the extent of $20,000 worth. These are not big items, but they are articles which have not been sold there before by Canadian exporters. There were $15,000 worth of rubber shoes and $14,750 worth of storage batteries sold. Eighteen new agencies were established during the year in the Argentine republic. The market was investigated on certain items for eighty-eight different firms who asked for investigations. Our total exports to the Argentine republic in 1928 amounted to $11,085,000 and I think in 1929 Mr. McColl was able to show

an increase from $11,085,000 to $14,493,000. I feel that as respects our exports to the Argentine, a country which is competitive with us in regard to wheat and other grain products but not with regard to manufactured products, the result of Mr. MoCoM's work of the year has been very satisfactory.
I notice among the list of agencies read by the minister, he does not mention Newfoundand. Are there any commercial agencies in Newfoundland?
We have no trade commissioners in Newfoundland.

Does the minister not think that a trade commissioner in Newfoundland rnuld secure a great deal more business for his country than a trade commissioner in Chicago? This is one of our own dominions vithin a short distance, especialfy of the maritime provinces, which imports practically all the manufactured articles and a great deal of the food products it uses. I am told that the bulk of its imports to-day is from the United States, of the very articles which could be supplied by Canada. There has been of late a great deal of discussion in the newspapers with reference to Canadian trade with Newfoundland, and all the articles are condemning the government of Canada for not appointing a trade agent in Newfoundland and going over to the cities of the United States where the markets are practically closed against us, establishing agencies there and letting trade that is right at our own doors be captured by the United States. This is a matter that the Department of Trade and Commerce could very well look into. The trade that is nearest home is always the most satisfactory to have. We could supply many of the commodities that the people of Newfoundland are to-day importing from the United States; but if the government does not think that trade is worth looking after and prefers to establish agencies in Chicago and other United States cities where the tariff is so high against us, I think the government is showing very poor business judgment. I thought I would draw the matter to the attention of the minister, because there are splendid opportunities for trade with Newfoundland.

We have looked upon Newfoundland as being a very easy country to reach, and one of our own men occasionally goes there to make a survey. At one time there was a trade commissioner's office in Newfoundland and a former minister thought it advisable to close the office because there was not enough work to keep the trade com-EMr. Malcolm.]
missioner busy. We had contemplated, if we succeeded in making a proper tariff agreement with Newfoundland, reopening an office. Our business with Newfoundland is not very difficult to look after and it is hard for a man in that country to find enough work to keep him busy. He has not much travelling to do because the business is practically all in the one city, namely, St. John and it is in the hands of a limited number of firms. Our trade with Newfoundland amounts to about $11,000,000 and is quite substantial.

It might be double that
amount.

It might be, if the Newfoundland firms found it profitable to import from Canada. My hon. friend will realize that Canada has not had any favourable tariff consideration from Newfoundland in the past. The rate of duty is the same on a Canadian article as on a United States article and it is not always easy for the Canadian exporter to increase his business. We are suggesting that Newfoundland should give us an empire preference. If that were done we would probably be justified in opening an office there.

Is it not a fact that Newfoundland just recently tried to negotiate a trade agreement with this country but did not meet with very much success? Did their Prime Minister not visit Ottawa within the last few months and go away very much discouraged with the reception he got in regard to trade relations?

I do not quite like the
idea of miy hon. friend from Digby trying to encourage the minister to establish a trade agency in Newfoundland. My experience from a business point of view is that wherever these trade commissioners have meddled, they have interfered with trade instead of benefiting it. My own company, coming down to personal matters, are presently and for a number of years have been doing a very fine trade with Newfoundland. Formerly we did a fine trade with France before the government monkeyed with it, but when they made their French treaty they cut us off entirely from the French market, and that is my reason for saying that I would very much prefer them to leave Newfoundland alone.

If they are going to
make a treaty, yes.

Yes, because I am not at all sure of the benefits of their treaty-making.

Every one they have
made has been a failure.

The minister a few minutes ago stated the amount of canned salmon that had been sold in New York owing to representations made by our office there. I would like to inquire whether this was imported into the United States for home consumption. or was reexported from the United States. The minister also said that a considerable trade had been worked up in biscuits.
A small trade.

My objection to opening
offices in the United States is based on my experience. Whenever my company or any other company that I ever had anything to do with worked up a business in the United States, just as soon as we got the business established, the United States immediately shut off the whole thing by raising the tariff overnight, and I say that simply to open an office in a country like that is an impossible business proposition. It is not right to spend the money on it, because we do not get any lasting benefit from it. I know that, and the minister knows it just as well as I do.

The minister can speak
feelingly on that point.

Very likely, if he has had anything like the experience that I have had.
I have got so that I leave it alone entirely.
I do not want any Canadian money spent in opening up offices in the United States, in Chicago or anywhere else. You can waste money enough without doing that. My experience has been that just as soon as you work up a trade with the United States it is shot to pieces overnight by an increase in their tariff, and they do not have to wait for congress to meet to raise the tariff.

I wish to offer a suggestion to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and that is a method by which he might	save	this	whole expenditure. Iassume that this vote is in the estimates for the purpose of helping Canadian business and Canadian business men. My hon. friend himself is a well-known business man, and I think	he	will	agree with my suggestionprivately, although he may not publicly; that is to	cut	out	this	item altogether and tomake	a move	that	will cost this country
nothing but will bring about far better results than the expenditure of this 8750,000 for trade agencies in foreign countries. Let us treat *other countries in tariff matters as they treat
us. That is my personal opinion of what we should do. By doing that we would hold the home market, and even if our people did not get the foreign markets because of foreign tariffs, we would get the home market, and in all probability, knowing our attitude, foreign countries would not raise their tariffs so high against us, and we would therefore increase our trade with foreign countries as well, and all that could be done without the expenditure of this money. I am not suggesting cutting out the vote. I am suggesting a method of supplementing the minister's efforts to obtain trade with foreign countries, and that is to treat other countries in tariff matters as they treat us, which would enable us to hold our own home market and get much more of the foreign market than we otherwise would do, because foreign countries then would not treat us with as little consideration as they now do.

There is not a man in
this house who is better able to protect his business thlan the minister, and there is no greater protectionist. His business enjoys the highest rate of protection that the Canadian tariff affords. That is true; the minister need not shake his head. In addition to that, he sees to it that a considerable proportion of his raw material comes in free. I do not think that the hon. member who has jusit spoken can teach the minister very much about protecting the interests of his own business. I leave that for the consideration of the minister and of the committee.

I was rather interested in noticing that we had two offices in South America. I have sometimes thought, and I wonder, if the minister has, that there are good possibilities of increasing our trade there. It has appeared to me that possibly the South American countries offer the most promising field for our exports in many lines of goods that we can find in the world to-day. While, of course, the minister undoubtedly understands his business a good deal better than I do, still for my part at least I would strongly encourage him to reach out into that field and do as much business there as possible. I think if he established three or more live trade agencies there, it would be money well spent. I think we could build up a very much larger business there than we now have. As a matter of fact, as far as I can see, the countries of South America and the Orient are about the two best directions which are now open to us in seeking new markets or extending the markets we now have.

I would like to supplement, the observations of tihe hon. member for Red Deer. Looking over the world at large, if we are going to trade we must make up our minds that we can trade only in those countries where there is the opportunity of selling what we produce. That means that we must sell primarily to those countries that do not produce what we have to sell. That seems to be axiomatic. We start with that, and what are we doing? We start two new offices this year in the United States, one in Chicago and one in San Francisco, and the next thing we find is that the United States increases its tariff on many of the goods that we could sell to them. The3' are increasing their tariff on beef and other agricultural products, on milk, for instance, and cream. By the elastic provisions of their tariff they can raise their tariff without waiting for legislation. All this is going on. I submit to the minister that in South America there is a very great opportunity, and while we are sitting by, the Americans are invading and securing that market. I think it is not too much to say , that in a large way the South Americans would sooner trade with the Canadians than with almost any other people they know, or I will put it this way: Other things being equal, they would give us the preference. I think the minister will say that is so. The office at Panama is highly desirable, also at Buenos Aires, Valparaiso, Lima and up the west coast of South America. AH these are very desirable, but when we talk of opening offices in the United States I put this to the minister: He is a manufacturer and he heard the hon. member from Lincoln, who is also a manufacturer, give his experience, and while this is not an experience meeting, because the experiences cannot at all be equal owing to the various businesses and the various tariffs imposed against them, may I say that during the last five years we have every evidence that when Canadian manufactured goods have found a market in the United States that market has been closed to them by the United States tariff, either by changing the classification or by a presidential proclamation, under their elastic tariff provisions, that shut our goods out.
That is true.

That was the intention
of the tariff aot of the United States. It was put there for that purpose. Therefore let us dtevote our time and our energy and our money to promoting trade in those portions of the world where there is an opportunity fMr. Speakman.]
for Canadian products to find a ready market. May I suggest to the minister that if he just had the same desire to promote trade in Canada as he has outside of Canada-
Yes, I have.

I would like to see the
evidence of it.

That is not my job
with these estimates.

The minister says that is not his job. Others may think that it is his job. But at any rate I do put this to him: has the time not come when the Canadian government of the day should be considering something in regard to the home market? There is $800,000,000 worth of trade that many people in Canada could get by going after it. We import over $1,360,000,000. Last year alone we imported $420,000,000 of iron and steel products. Take electric goods; we send our copper blister to be refined in the United States, and because we have to pay a quarter of a cent a pound more than their own manufacturers pay for the same copper, we buy electric goods made in the United States. The same thing applies to nickel, to asbestos and to various other materials. The development of export trade is highly desirable; but remember this, in developing export trade we are subject to the caprice and the jealousy and the competition of the countries to which we ship our goods, as well as competition from every other country in the world. On the other hand-, we have a market at home which last year we threw away to the extent of $11300,000,000.
Oh, no.

But that is what it gets down to. Do you realize that last year in duties alone on goods imported we collected $200,000,000. That was half of the entire revenue of the Dominion. If the minister will display the same interest in Canadian trade that he shows in his own business, and see that Canadian trade is protected by a tariff similar to that which he enjoys, then our manufacturers will have the business. I put that to him as a Canadian business man of whom we are proud, because he has succeeded in his business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are getting personal.
No, we are proud of him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So are we.

He has succeeded. Why? Because he has had an opportunity of fair competition with the whole world. How did he get it? He did not get it; his business got it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave it to his business-a protection of 30 per cent. The minister's steel, his iron, his logs, his raw material come in free.
Oh, no.

Not wholly, perhaps, but partly. The steel and iron from which you make your castors, the logs out of which you saw your ebony, your mahogany, your teak, your oak-these things come in free', and the reason that a profitable business has been built up in Kincardine, of which this country has some reason to be proud, is that the protection given to this Canadian industry has ensured that it will be maintained in this country against the mass production of the world.
Now, I want the minister to spend a little of his splendid talent and his energy and his vision in doing something for Canada; instead of trying to sell goods in the United States by trade commissioners in New York, in Chicago, and in San Francisco, and then when they get the business opened up, " bing," as the boy says, up goes the tariff, and that is the end of it. I know a case where a Canadian manufacturer established a market in Michigan. He said: "Here is my chance for my surplus product.'' He made his goods in Toronto, but before he could get his order actually delivered in Michigan the tariff classification became such that those goods could not be despatched. Right within five miles of where I now stand is a factory that tried to make aviation suits for sale in the United States, but the classification was so changed that they could not be shipped into that market. The people of the United States are not going to let Canada invade their market. To keep out our goods they change their classification overnight. I suggest to the minister that he devote some of his splendid talent to looking after our home market. He is a protectionist; the Minister of National Revenue is a protectionist; the Minister of Justice is a Genevaite-that is a little different: the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is a collector of curios-and he would certainly like to have a free trader as a curio; the Secretary of State is a protectionist-
Complete the picture.

Well the member for
North Battleford is neither.

Mr. Chairman, I am in sympathy with the Minister of Trade and Commerce in opening up trade agencies in the United States. Contrary to what has been said by the front-benchers of the opposition, trade has been developed with the United States in spite of their high tariffs.
In what?

In certain
agricultural products. The export of cream and milk from this country to the United States has increased in spite of the raising of the tariff ever since the defeat of the Wilson administration.
Does the hon. gentleman know that on the 18th day of this month it will be increased by 50 per cent?

Yes; but the records will show-my hon. friend can get them and they will prove my contention- that in spite of all the tariff increases on cream and milk there has been a steady increase in our export of these commodities to the United States. I cannot understand the logic of the front-benchers of the Conservative party when they claim to be a high tariff party, and yet say that the raising of the tariff in the United States shoots business all to pieces. It must be a poor rule that does not work both ways. They would raise our tariff to a high level, and then our international trade would be shot to pieces. Surely we realize that in this day and age no nation can live unto itself alone, that we have to be traders the world over.
Does the hon. gentleman realize that we lost $100,000,000 worth of export business to the United States the first year the Fordney-McCumber tariff came into effect?
I admit that it affects our trade for a certain time.
It will be four times that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But we are still very
much alive.

Our exports
of certain farm products to the United States have increased steadily in spite of their raising the tariff at different times. I have observed that the leader of the opposition in asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce to apply to his department many of the principles he applies to his own business, said that a lot of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
his raw materials came in free. I believe one reason why the business of the minister has grown and prospered is that he has been able to assess the Canadian consumer to the extent of about 35 per cent on his output.

I do not think my hon.
friend will mind being corrected. There never was a duty of 35 per cent on furniture. It is only 30 per cent. The British preferential tariff is 18 per cent. In a great many instances the Canadian furniture manufacturers take no notice whatever of the duty; they sell their goods on a cost-plus-profit basis, and you will find a great many articles of furniture sold at the same price in Canada as in the United States.

Then why do you need
the duty?
In my speech on the budget I took our imports of furniture and the duty collected thereon-the average duty under all tariffs-and I know that the average duty was over 25 per cent.
That may be.
That was on actual transactions, not figuring out the percentages at all. If that is so, our furniture manufacturers are accorded that amount of protection.

I hope my hon. friend
is not arguing that because there is a tariff of 25 per cent on a commodity, the Canadian manufacturer takes advantage of that tariff. He must not argue that way. Every automobile tire is about the same price in Canada and the United States, and that can be shown in regard to commodity after commodity. My hon. friend is not fair if he arrives at that conclusion.

I might be
if I did not have specific instances to which I might refer. We know that in 1926 there was a slight reduction of about 10 per cent on automobiles and the price was immediately reduced. Had they not taken advantage of the tariff there would have been no price reduction. Whenever there is a reduction in the tariff there is a corresponding reduction in price. In this house only a short time ago, during this session, the classification of combines reduced the tariff from 10 per cent to 6 per cent. What happened in the west? Many combines had been sold, but the purchasers have received notice that the amount they will have to pay will be less by $60 to $100, although the contract of sale has already been made. This is due simply to the fact that the tariff was reduced from 10 to 6 per cent.
Where are they made?

I can show
that on several occasions when the tariff has been reduced there has been a reduction in price, and that to me is proof positive that many of these duties are taken advantage of by the manufacturers. The hon. member for Leeds says that combines are not made here. They are made by the Massey-Harris Company.
Of the United States.

In other words, they import from Canada 51.51 gallons of whiskey for each inhabitant of the island who is not at school. There are 600 children at school in the island, and if they stayed at home and drank as much whiskey as all the adults of the island there would be consumed 42 gallons of whiskey for each man, woman and child in Miquelon-and this is exclusive of the amount of malt beer and whiskey imported from other countries. In Canada the per capita consumption is .31, or one-third of a gallon per head, as compared with 51.51 per head of the population of that little island. Now the curious fact is that the value of Canadian whiskey in Miquelon is only $5.50 a gallon, according to the reports of the department, compared with $16 in the United States. It seems to me that these trade commissioners must be very enthusiastic when they operate in small islands. For instance, in the West Indies, all the large islands consume only a limited quantity of Canadian whiskey, while the small islands consume about the same proportion as the island of Miquelon; and the price of whiskey in the West Indies is $5 a gallon. If a gallon of whiskey goes direct to the United States we get an excise duty of $9 per gallon on it; when it goes to these small islands the people there get it without paying this duty, there being no excise nor export duty in this case. The Minister of Finance does not make a budget any more in this country; he does not know what the previous year has done for him, and he does not make a budget at all for the next year. He does not even make a guess at it. We have stopped budgeting so far as this parliament is concerned.

I wish to thank the
minister for the very sympathetic view he takes of the matter. No doubt he will recall that at an annual meeting of the manufacturers' association six or eight years ago this matter was discussed very fully and a strong memorandum was directed to the various governments. If the minister would take such action as he suggests, and call the attention of the various provincial governments to the desirability of a uniform system in this regard, the reform could be affected within a reasonable time, to the great advantage of trade and to the satisfaction of all who are in any way interested in statistics affecting the commerce of the country.

So far as trade figures
are concerned, there is a publication which has been issued for a good many years now giving the figures annually.

The real truth is, as the hon. member for Pictou has pointed out, that people abroad find it difficult to follow our statistics. Our railway accounts end with the calendar year, and our public accounts with March 31. The result is that the House of Commons will not be in a position for another year to discuss the expenditure made by this government for the year ended March 31, 1929. That is the real difficulty. The minister will recall that we changed it once from October, and then to June and back to March. Certainly in the provinces the same difficulty has been experienced-and it relates to the calling of parliament or the legislature. The real reason behind the present system is that the Auditor General's report may be available in order that the accounts may be as fresh as possible. The fact of the matter is that we have not had a budget speech since Mr. Fielding made his last. Mr. Fielding of course always made a budget speech; he budgetted for the year ending March 31 of the next year. The present Minister of Finance will not take a chance and estimate what his revenue and expenditure will be; he votes his money, but he has never made an.estimate of the revenue since Mr. Fielding's budget of 1923. In British Columbia they estimate their revenue by departments, and they deal in the same way with their expenditure. They make a complete budget statement showing the expected revenue from each department of the public service, together with a statement of contemplated expenditures of each department, and their public accounts are prepared accordingly. In recent years the Dominion government has not been doing this and the situation is getting worse, with the result that people outside the country find it difficult to follow our accounts. The League of Nations has been endeavouring to secure uniformity in this matter. The Minister of Labour, through the representation which Canada will have, should be able to secure a system of uniform accounts, particularly with the aid of the Minister of Justice. But this has not been done. All we have been able to do is to get a uniform policy with respect to free trade, which some hon. gentlemen say it is desirable to follow but which the Minister of Finance says is no good. Cannot the Minister of Labour do something for us?

The Canadian government motion picture bureau was organized in 1917 and operates as a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Its functions are: To produce and circulate throughout the world motion pictures and iphatographic material designed to disseminate information about Canada, its resources, opportunities, scenic beauties, attractions, basic industries and so on, and through this means encourage development, trade, settlement and tourist travel; as a central organization for the production of technical, instructional, advertising and other such types of films and pictorial material for all federal government departments; to cooperate with the provincial governments, the national railways and steamship lines and other organizations in the production of all types of pictorial matter used for the general development of the Dominion's interests, welfare and progress; to cooperate with the motion picture industry in matters pertaining to the general development, welfare and (progress of the Dominion.
Since its organization in 1917 the bureau each year has shown steady and substantial development, both in the scope and extent of its activities and the volume of pictorial matter produced and distributed. During the present fiscal year the bureau has shown the greatest growth in every branch of its work of any year in its history. The total volume of motion pictures prepared and processed will, if is estimated, exceed the previous year's total by approximately 20 per cent, and the total amount of other photographic material produced and distributed will exceed the previous year's total by approximately 25 per cent. The total number of films in circulation throughout the world on January 31 of this year is approximately 80 per cent greater than at the same date a year previous. The extent and coverage of territory, while not definitely estimable, is vastly greater than for any other year.

Mr. Chairman, I have one criticism to make which applies not only to this department, but to others, and I think it is one to which the minister will listen with rMr. Malcolm.]
sympathy. It is very advisable that our advertising should preserve a continuity regardless of administration; whether a Liberal government be in power, or a Conservative or Labour government be in power, is not a matter of importance. The Empire Marketing Board has been doing some very wonderful advertising in connection with Canada through the medium of hampers which are packed with Canadian goods and which can be purchased at the corner grocery. In each basket or hamper there is a statement as to how much Great Britain purchased from Canada, and how much Canada purchased from them; the number of men who went to the war from Canada, and other interesting information. While in England I took the trouble to go into this matter very carefully and I was struck with the character of the advertising and the appeal it must make to the people interested. Certain departments have been issuing advertising with the name of the minister or the deputy minister attached, and I suggest to the minister, in the best spirit in the world, that these advertisements which are issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce of Canada should be issued by the department and should not contain any person's name. In England they have found that the preservation of the continuity of the advertising is the one thing to be observed and when, in a very short time, the people have an opportunity to place another government in power these advertisements will be issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce of the Dominion of Canada. This matter has been brought to my attention on more than one occasion and it has been said that the Department of the Interior, the Department of Trade and Commerce, and one or two other departments have issued advertisements of that character. I should like very much to be able to assure him that I could dictate to the conference, but I do not know any minister of trade and commerce in the past who has tried to do it and not come to grief.

You tried it a couple of
years ago.

I would point out to the minister that in 1925 his right hon. leader in his celebrated declaration from Richmond Hill told the country that there would be no monopoly on land or sea, that the north Atlantic conference would be brought to account at once, and that there were to be fair rates accorded' to everyone on land and sea. Since then I understand the Canadian government merchant marine has twice increased its rates, cooperating with the conference. J

Before the minister answers, I would suggest that there is no good reason why he should fear the fate that overtook his predecessor in office in an endeavour to deal with this problem. His desire for office is not so great, I am sure, as to discourage him from venturing upon the field where a certain distinguished gentleman met his Waterloo. The minister should deal with the point brought up by the hon. member for Digby. Knowing his ability to secure appropriations for North Bruce to provide steamship connections from the most remote ports in that peninsula with the outside world, surely he is not going to neglect the apple shippers of Nova Scotia for the sake of the local traffic of North Bruce. If he displays the same energy in dealing with that situation as he has in securing rebates on coal used in the salt works in his constituency, and in securing appropriations for public works in the most remote part of the North Bruce peninsula, I am sure he will be able to secure substantial results for the Nova Sootia apple shippers.

people who theoretically condemn the conference rates. But I have very grave doubts whether their position in relation to the United States shippers would be improved if such action were taken.

But the major part of
the United States traffic out of New York is carried in British bottoms.
Yes.

They do not object to the
rate of 90 cents per barrel, but they do object to being penalized if they do not use the federation steamers exclusively. For instance, if a shipper wants to ship his apples this week by the federation boat, and next week desires to ship by another line, he is charged $1.10 per barrel instead of 90 cents unless he gives them the entire shipment. If the statement made
by the hon. member is correct there is an instrument ready to hand for the minister to wield. I submit that the situation indicated by the hon. member is intolerable. One resents an injustice. If A is charged half what B is compelled to pay then B has a right to insist upon fair treatment; and the government is there to see that fair treatment is meted out. The matter now is with the minister. This is a matter of transportation, a matter of trade and commerce, and it is within his jurisdiction.

The minister has a

If I do not ship all my apples one way I am to be penalized by paying twenty cents a barrel more in order to get them to the other side? We have wharves and railways, and we should teach these people that, while we will utilize their facilities for the purpose of shipping apples, when it suits us, if someone else comes forward who will take our apples at the same rate, we will use the facilities they afford, and no one shall put a pistol to our heads and say, "All or none."

I think my hon. friend is referring to the waiving of the coastal regulations in the fall to permit the storage of grain in boats over the winter. All I can say to the house is that every fall there has been a pressure brought by those moving grain to take advantage of all the available space that can be found. That pressure undoubtedly comes from the shippers who wish to allow American boats to load grain and hold it in storage at the bay ports for unloading during the winter or spring. The coastal regulations call for the unloading of the boat during the season of navigation; to allow the boat to remain with a cargo is a violation of the coastal regulations and requires the passing of an order in council. These orders in council have been passed for the last several years on the recommendations of the Board of Grain Commissioners, in an endeavour to provide additional space, and the Lake Carriers' Association, which I believe has made complaints to the hon. member for Kingston, naturally objects to this practice.
So far as my department is concerned, and so far as I personally am concerned, I do not see that any great harm has been done to the Canadian shippers; as a matter of fact I think some good has been done the handlers of grain by allowing them to take advantage of this extra space. It is quite possible that it is a mistake to let so much grain come down; it is quite possible that the opinion held by some that there is altogether too much grain in our

show window and not enough back in the warehouse, to use the vernacular, is well taken.
