I have been taking up with the minister a number of times a matter in connection with the tax on canoes, rowboats and motorboats in Muskoka. If the minister will be good enough to tell me that he will repeal the order in council in question, I shall have nothing more to say.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Unfortunately I am
not in a position to be as generous as that in regard to my hon. friend's request. I should like to hear his reasons.

I am sorry the minister cannot give me that assurance. I will ask

him another question, because I do not want to say anything that is unnecessary with regard to this matter. Has the government determined to leave that order in council in force?
That is practically what has been decided. There may be a discussion and a reduction of the rates, but I am afraid we shall have to stand by the order in council.

Then I shall have to
enter a protest against the discrimination that is being exercised in connection with the riding which I have the honour to represent. I do not know why my riding should be singled out from all the ridings of the Dominion of Canada and an order in council passed imposing a tax of from $1 to $8 on all canoes, rowboats and motor boats. I know what the minister will say, namely, that this has been asked for by a tourist association some of whom, I am free to admit, are Conservatives, but I humbly submit to the minister that it would be better to take advice, if he is going for advice to Conservatives at all, from those who represent the people rather than from those who do not represent anybody. I submit that this tax is unfair and discriminatory, because in the whole Dominion of Canada it is only my riding that has been singled out. Moreover, this is a tax which it is impossible to enforce. Let me read for the minister's information his own order in council, so that I shall have a basis for the remarks I intend to make:
His Excellency the governor general in counoil, on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and under the provisions of the Government Harbours and Piers Act, chapter 89 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered that the regulations made and established by order in council, P.C. 1170 dated 12th July, 1928, be applied to the following waters to be known as the harbour of Muskoka lakes-

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
To be defined as follows:
All the waters of lakes Muslcoka, Rousseau and Joseph, including their connecting and tributary waters.
I wonder if the minister has ever considered what that means. We have three lakes there with a coastline of possibly 200 miles that he is going to make into a harbour. More than that he is taking in all the tributary rivers and the connecting waters-for example, the south branch of the Muskoka river, which runs away back into the district of Haliburton, and the north branch, which runs away up into the district of Parry Sound. The other outlet from the lake runs into Georgian bay. Taking it all in all, I think his order in council is making a harbour that will have from 1,000 to 1,500 miles of coastline. If that is not a ridiculous thing to do, I do not know what would be. Moreover, it is an infliction that is going to penalize not only the ordinary residents of Muskoka but tourists as well. The tourist trade is bringing a large amount of money into this country every year; in a former debate it was estimated at $275,000,000 a year. If these regulations are going to be enforced, every tourist who comes to this country will have to hunt up some person, take an affidavit, go and get a license, put number plates on his boats or canoes, and equip them with lights. That will be a real annoyance to the many tourists who come into our country, many of them bringing a canoe on the side of their car. It will be a real annoyance also to the farmers and other residents of Muskoka living near the Muskoka lakes.
If the minister will read the regulations he will find that they require a light to be carried in the stern of a boat or canoe that will be visible from all sides. If the minister has ever been in a row boat or a canoe, he must know that that is impossible. No man could fix a light in the stern of a boat so that it would be visible from all sides on a dark night. These regulations are going to be a worse nuisance than the luxury taxes which the Conservatives put on years ago, and they are bound to cause an immense amount of trouble. Only one man is appointed to issue the licenses; he lives in Toronto nine months out of twelve, and during the other three months he is located in the little village of Port Carling. People will have to go miles and miles to get their number plates and licenses. It will mean that some people will have to go from fifty to sixty or seventy miles.
The minister has been very generous in saying that he will reconsider this matter.
I am going to be frank with him: he could not put in my hands a better instrument to get votes than these regulations if they are to be enforced. But I am not looking at it from that point of view; I am looking at it from the point of view of the good of the country. The tourist trade is rapidly growing, and petty annoyances of this sort will disgust those who come to visit this country. The tax, it is true, runs only from $1 to $8, but it is heavy. The government does not get a cent out of it, because all the money is turned over to a man who is appointed as harbour commissioner, a man who is an outsider and the people up there are estimating that he will draw from $6,000 to $10,000 a year.
The regulations are going to be a real nuisance, and will not react to the credit of this government. Many of my people, farmers scattered along the shore line of the lakes, miles and miles away from a village, have two or three canoes or rowboats, and they have to go to all this trouble simply to appease Sir Thomas W hite and othei people like him who were instrumental in persuading the government that this was the right thing to do, when it is really the wrong thing to do. I am not blaming the government for it, but they should not have listened to this advice. The object of making these boats carry lights is, of course, the protection of life, but I submit that under the law as it stands everything can be obtained that the minister is seeking to obtain here, and with a great deal less trouble. I am going to ask the minister and the government to repeal these regulations.
Reducing the cost of the license will help some, but that is not all the trouble. When you look at the penalties that are attached, you will see that a man may be imprisoned for not carrying a license number on his boat or canoe or motor boat. When a man brings his canoe or rowboat in to the shore at night he invariably turns it upside down to let the water out. If there are electric batteries in the boat they are likely to tumble out and get wet unless they are permanently fastened. As I said a few minutes ago, if I were seeking my own. political advantage I would say nothing and let the government proceed to enforce these regulations, and the more strictly they were enforced the better it would be for me politically. But I say I am looking at it from the point of view of the good of the country, especially a country so closely tied up with the tourist traffic as Muskoka is. I hesitate very much to accept even in a

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
modified form anything that is going to be such an irritation. I ask the minister and the government, who have been very kind and considerate with regard to all my requests, to see if they cannot cancel this order.

May ,1 direct the minister's attention to what I conceive to be the legal position in connection with this matter? The order in council purports to 'be made under the provisions of chapter 89 of the revised statutes of Canada. The title of that chapter is " An Act respecting the government harbours, piers and breakwaters," and the act may be cited as " the Government Harbours and Piers Act." In this act, "minister" means the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Section 3 reads:
Nothing in this act shall apply to the harbour of Toronto, Quebec, Montreal, Halifax, Pictou, or St. John, New Brunswick, or any harbour under the management of commissioners appointed under any act of the parliament of Canada.
That in itself indicates the meaning that is to be attached to the word "harbour" generally. Then section 4 says, with respect to works under the control of the minister:
Excepting such wharfs, piers and breakwaters as are on or connected with oanals, the use, maintenance and ordinary repairs of all harbours, wharfs, piers and breakwaters constructed or completed at the expense of Canada, or in any way the property of Canada, and the making and enforcing of regulations concerning such use, maintenance and ordinary re,pairs, and the collection of tolls and dues for such use, shall be under the control and management of the minister.
The powers of the governor in council are set out in section 6:
The governor in council may appoint or direct such officers or persons as he thinks proper, who shall have, under the direction of the minister, the charge of the works by this act placed under the management and control of the minister, and who shall collect the tolls and dues to be paid in respect thereof.
That refers to tolls and dues in connection with harbour works. Subsection 2 of section 6 reads:
The governor in council may determine the remuneration to be allowed them respectively for such services, and such remuneration shall J>e retained from the tolls and dues collected.
Then section 7 provides that 'the governor in council may make regulations. Section 8 deals with the publication of the regulations, section 9 with the collection of tolls, and how enforced, and section 10 provides that no clearance shall be granted to vessels unless the tolls are paid. I think the Minister of Justice, who is beside the minister, will agree that unless there is a grant of power by parliament upon the minister and or the governor in
fMr. McGibbon.]
council to make regulations no regulations may validly be made. That is clear. There must be a grant of power to permit the regulations to be legally made.
Under the order in council the minister purports to convert one thousand miles of lake and river front into a harbour. These words occur in paragraph (1) of the order in council:
That the regulations made and established by order in council P.C. 1170 dated 12tli July, 1928, be applied to the following waters to be known as the harbour of Muskoka lakes:
Imagine, Mr. Minister of Justice, an order in council purporting to convert a river and lake shore front extending over one thousand miles into a harbour to be called the harbour of Muskoka lakes, the description being as follows:
All the waters of lakes Muskoka, Rousseau and Joseph, including their connecting and tributary waters.
That becomes the harbour. The whole basis of this new regulation is that a harbour lias been established with respect to which these tolls may be applied. Certainly there is no grant of power by this parliament to the governor in council to make that regulation. There is nothing within the four corners of this statute that confers upon the governor in council power to make a harbour, and much less would council have power to make a harbour of the Muskoka lakes. The word "harbour" must have the ordinary designation attaching to it, as is shown in the use of the expression "harbour of Montreal, harbour of Quebec," and so on. Now the government is going to make three lakes and the connecting rivers into a harbour called "Muskoka harbour." The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is a professional man, and he has beside him the departmental adviser. I think he will agree that the leading cases in the privy council 'hold that parliamentary authorization is necessary to the validity of an order in council.

Of course not. Then I just make this request of the minister, and he and I will have no further argument about it: show me within the four corners of the statute the power to make this order in council.

Before this discussion
closes, I should point out that there are a number of people interested besides the member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon). The minister attempts to call the Muskoka lakes and. their tributary waters a harbour. Well, a part of those waters extend up into Algonquin park and into my riding. Mani-

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
festly it would be unfair that a man travelling along the highway beyond, say, Parry Sound, carrying a canoe on his car, should be compelled to have attached to that canoe one of the lights suggested by the minister and to buy a license for his craft if he wants to use it on any little stream tributary to the Muskoka lakes. If the minister wanted to do it piecemeal he could have secured orders in council dealing with the Trent river, the Muskoka river and the French river systems. Therefrom he would derive an unwarranted revenue for the government. It is absolutely right that regulations should be made to provide that motor and other boats carry lights at night when they are running through crowded or dangerous waters; there is no objection to that at all. But if a farmer in that country has some ten, fifteen or twenty canoes that he hires out during the tourist season, and perhaps a few motor boats, he is taxed between $20 and $150 under this order in council as now proposed by the minister. The whole proposal is absolutely unfair, it is class legislation, and there is no justification for it. I agree with the leader of the opposition that no such proceeding is authorized by statute.

This is not a new question. For over ten years representations have been made to the Department of Marine and Fisheries to take action to prevent the possibility of accidents on these lakes where there is a somewhat heavy traffic of motor and rowboats, particularly at night. Representations have also been made to the department by people who are interested in navigation on the Muskoka lakes. A few years ago the petitioners were supported by the municipal bodies of the localities! surrounding those lakes. The government did not act on its own volition with a view to imposing nuisance taxes, as my hon. friend from Muskoka said. We simply desired to meet a request which has been made to us on many occasions. I can see now that the opinions of certain people have changed since that time, but I think that everybody will admit it is quite proper to take the necessary steps to protect life on these lakes, particularly at night when very fast motor boats are likely to place in a very dangerous position those using canoes, rowboats and even small motor boats.

I do not think that either the member for Muskoka-Ontario or myself has any objection to a regulation to safeguard the public or the users of motor and rowboats and canoes. What we are objecting to is that the government in passing this order in council went further than any request that they received from any organization in
Muskoka or any other part of the Dominion, and imposed a very substantial tax upon the owners and users of boats in that section. If the government want to appoint a man to enforce the present law regarding the carrying of lights at night by motor and other boats, I shall be satisfied as I am sure will be my hon. friend from Muskoka.

Will the minister elaborate the point raised by the leader of the opposition? What is his authority to declare any body of water a harbour? The act does not give him any power. Here are three or four large lakes and adjacent rivers. We know they do not constitute a harbour. Under what authority does the minister declare those large bodies of water to be a harbour? Parliament might do it, but he has no power.

May I say in reply that
a large body of water may be termed a harbour, as well as a small body. The extent of the water does not signify.

Who has the right to
declare it to be a harbour?
We have the right according to the law under which we have acted.
What section?

My hon. friend the leader
of the opposition stressed certain words, " piers and breakwaters." But he left aside the general wording of the act respecting government harbours.
No, he mentioned that.

Yes, but he argued more
particularly that piers and breakwaters referred to works which have been constructed.

Where is the power to
make this body of water a harbour?

The power under which we acted is contained in section 7:
The governor in council may, on the recommendation of the minister, make rules and regulations for the use -and management of such harbours, wharves, piers and breakwaters, and a tariff or tariffs.

Manifestly this area is
not a harbour unless it is so declared by some power. The word " harbour " has a definite meaning in the English language. Parliament might do it.

Have the law officers of the crown been consulted about this matter? As the Minister of Justice knows, the only harbours that the Dominion has any power over at all are the "public harbours" as described in the third schedule of the British North

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
America Act. My hon. friends the two ministers ought to know the situation very well in view of the Montreal harbour commissioners' case which went through the courts here and then to the privy council. I wish I had had an opportunity of looking up that case; but the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will find that the word "harbour" is discussed in that very case. Certainly a series of lakes is not a harbour. But where do you get your authority? It must come from the British North America Act, and the specific description there is "public harbours." What is a harbour? A harbour is a place where ships ride into anchor. It is not a lake over which ships ply; it is not a sea over which ships ply; and to undertake to pass a law of this description, and then visit penalties if it is not kept, seems to me, frankly, ridiculous. I cannot believe that any law officer of the crown has been consulted in reference to this order in council. I respect law, and I sometimes think that even a poor law should have some respect; but I tell you plainly that I would advise any of these men in that district, in this great series of lakes, who found themselves offended by this order in council to disobey it and to, take the government of the country, at the expense of the government, through the law courts. It has been done before. I think that before this is relied upon we are entitled as a parliament to have the statement of someone learned in the law who will say that this is a proper order in council and within the power of the Dominion of Canada. You cannot deal with anything but public harbours because you have not property in anything else, and the British North America Act is specific.

Not to prolong the discussion, or to expose the government to the possibility suggested by my hon. friend, I am ready to look into the matter again and to submit the case to the Department of Justice.
I thank the minister.

How many icebreakers are

We have the Lady Grey, the Mikula, the Montcalm and the Stanley. The Stanley, as my hon. friend knows, operates in Nova Scotia.

Has the minister anything to do with the law concerning the directorships of steamship companies? Of course the minister has nothing to do with the American law, but under their law a Canadian cannot be a director. In the formation of the board of directors of Canadian steamship companies this same rule does not apply, and I know of one case where only one

Canadian is on the board. I think the time has come when we should insist that the boards of directors of Canadian steamship companies should consist entirely of Canadians.

Item agTeed to.
To continue subsidies for wrecking plants-* Quebec and British Columbia, $45,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like
to renew my annual request that the government consider the increasing of this amount for British Columbia. The government subsidizes a very good wrecking plant, one of the best in the world, but it is stationed at
Esquimalt all the time. Esquimalt is at the south end of Vancouver island, and the plant is available for any part of the Pacific coast. But this plant is needed to a greater extent, especially in the winter months, on the west coast of Vancouver island, which is known as the graveyard of the Pacific. The government has attempted to meet this situation by maintaining a small gasoline lifeboat at Bamfield, and have supplemented that service in the winter months by maintaining one of the fishing patrol boats or one of the navy boats at that point. These boats are much too light for the work. They were mine sweepers during the war, but it would be useless for them to go out in a heavy sea and attempt to pull a steamer out of danger by towing it, or anything of that kind. The plant at Esquimalt is admirably suited for this purpose, and if a few thousand dollars were added to the vote a suitable plant could be maintained at Bamfield and (he government would have a life-saving service of which they would be proud. .The crews of the boats which are located there at present are very capable, seafaring men and I have no doubt that they would answer a call of distress under any conditions, and might possibly lose their lives. The fear has always been on my conscience, that we are asking these men to go out in boats which are not safe. This condition could be overcome by the government providing a few thousand dollars to meet the extra cost of keeping one of these fully equipped salvage boats on the west coast. Even if it were kept there for only two months i't might provide valuable service, as the other boats could serve for the remaining two months.

Why is it that this vote
includes only Quebec and British Columbia? Does the minister not realize that a little shipping comes in and out of the ports in the maritime provinces? Why are they neglected in subsidies of this kind? We have several wrecking plants in the maritime provinces, but I understand they are not included in this subsidy at all. If the maritime provinces can maintain wrecking plants, why cannot Quebec and British Columbia maintain their own wrecking plants without a subsidy; or if we are going to give a subsidy to those two provinces, why not give a subsidy to the maritime provinces? Why discriminate against them? Personally I do not think it is necessary for either Quebec or British Columbia to receive a subsidy. They could very well go without it and we could use that $45,000 for some better purpose. But if it is necessary to subsidize wrecking plants in those two provinces, it is just as necessary to subsidize

similar plants in the maritime provinces. I think gross discrimination is being shown in this regard.

We are not subsidizing
wrecking plants in the maritime provinces because the private companies there have enough work and a revenue large enough to take care of their plants and to operate them successfully. In British Columbia and Quebec they have not enough revenue to maintain the wrecking plants required for the safety of navigation, and that is why we give a subsidy to those companies.

With the shipping that goes
in and out of the Pacific ports and up the St. Lawrence river, I think wrecking plants should be able to be maintained there as profitably as they can be in the maritime provinces. I do not think the minister's answer is satisfactory at all. I know a number of wrecking plants in the maritimes have made no money whatever in the last few years; in fact several of them have been obliged to go out of business.

I suggest to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis that British Columbia might forego a share of that $45,000 in favour of the maritimes if they would give us our share of the $160,000 annually they have been keeping from our fishermen for the last forty years.

On the Pacific seaboard to-day, along Hecate straits, where the greatest fishing industry in Canada exists, where the majority of the fishermen who are the producers in this important industry are toiling, there are no life-saving facilities. I want to drive this home to the minister:	We who represent the fisher-folk
do not stand up in the House of Commons just for fun; we are here to advocate what we believe is essential, and I wish to say now that, as regards life-saving along the Pacific coast, the government has not done its duty to the men who go down to the sea in ships. There should be a further increase in this all-important vote and the British Columbia

coast should be included in it. It is natural for those who live in the eastern provinces remote from the sea to think the man who comes here and presents a picture of marine life, which is not merely wonderful in itself but which is full of the greatest dangers, adventures, and risks, is speaking of something which is trivial. Such is not the case. It is a great question and worthy of the consideration of every member of this House of Commons. What I want to bring out is this: we are voting $80,000 for life-saving for all Canada. I should like to ask:	How many
